An Algebraic View of the Expressivity of Recurrent Language Models

Franz Nowak Affiliation: ETH Zürich Correspondence to: franz.nowak@inf.ethz.ch    Ryan Cotterell Affiliation: ETH Zürich Correspondence to: ryan.cotterell@inf.ethz.ch    Reda Boumasmoud Affiliation: ETH Zürich Correspondence to: reda.boumasmoud@math.ethz.ch
Abstract

What formal languages can a recurrent neural language model recognize? Formal results in the literature conflict: some authors report Turing-completeness, while others show equivalence to regular languages. The reason for this discrepancy is that the underlying arithmetic model differs. The paper develops a unified algebraic account of the expressivity of recurrent neural networks, starting with a formal account of various arithmetic models. This account reduces expressivity to an algebraic question, e.g., whether a network’s syntactic monoid divides a certain wreath product. As a case study, the paper revisits diagonal state-space models: the same architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter once floating-point recurrences are enforced, yet realizes every even-modulus counter under unsigned-integer quantization.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML, RNN, SSM, Expressivity, Formal Languages, Algebra, Automata, Theory

1 Introduction

The recent proliferation and widespread adoption of neural language models for a wide range of text-based tasks, e.g., question answering (OpenAI, 2021), proving mathematical statements (Lewkowycz et al., 2022), and general-purpose reasoning (Wei et al., 2022; OpenAI, 2024), have motivated a formal study of their capabilities. A growing research program treats architectures such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformer language models as objects of classical computation theory (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1992; Weiss et al., 2018; Merrill, 2019; Hahn, 2020; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Pérez et al., 2021; Chiang and Cholak, 2022; Strobl et al., 2024, inter alia). They are studied as recognizers and generators of formal languages and classified by the computational resources they require. This line of work on RNN expressivity has led to tangible practical insights: For instance, Sarrof et al. (2024) showed that linear RNNs with nonnegative diagonal recurrences, such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024), cannot recognize languages that require maintaining a modulo counter over arbitrary lengths. This finding motivated the invention of more expressive linear RNNs (Grazzi et al., 2025).

Formal inquiry into the expressive power of neural language models, however, has produced seemingly contradictory conclusions. For example, it has been claimed that RNNs are Turing-complete (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1992). On the other hand, it has also been claimed that they can only simulate finite automata (Merrill, 2019). Both claims hold true, but, crucially, rely on different assumptions. For instance, some theoretical work assumes exact arithmetic over ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℚ\mathbb{Q} (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1992; Chen et al., 2018; Hahn, 2020; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Svete et al., 2024), some treat precision as an explicit resource (e.g., logarithmic growth in sequence length) (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2023; Karuvally et al., 2025), while others appeal to finite precision while leaving operational details of the arithmetic underspecified (Omlin and Giles, 1996; Weiss et al., 2018; Sarrof et al., 2024; Stogin et al., 2024). To characterize an architecture’s expressivity rigorously, these details must be fixed: the algebraic structure in which computation occurs, the representation of values, and the semantics of rounding, overflow, and evaluation order. Many proofs of expressivity implicitly rely on these identities and therefore do not automatically transfer to floating-point implementations. A central claim of this paper is that the underlying arithmetic semantics is part of the object being analyzed. It is an open question which assumptions are most appropriate for neural language models actually deployed in practice.

This paper brings together a variety of formal treatments of RNNs. Using concrete specifications of the underlying arithmetic model, we establish a purely algebraic characterization of recurrent architectures, unifying expressivity questions within an abstract framework. We show that arithmetic models with a finite set of possible values induce a finite, architecture-dependent transition monoid. In deep recurrent models, layers compose hierarchically, so multiple layers implement a cascade of algebraic cores. Algebraically, this cascade is a submonoid of the wreath product of the layer monoids. Expressivity questions then reduce to rigorous statements about the resulting monoid and its structure, recovering or refining many results in the literature as straightforward consequences. If any of the underlying assumptions change, such as the numerical semantics or the possible recurrence parametrization of a core, only this part needs to be adjusted while the remaining abstractions stay the same, greatly simplifying analysis.

We demonstrate the utility of our approach through a case study of diagonal SSMs, showing that different arithmetic semantics (numerical domain, rounding, evaluation order, etc.) give different expressivity results for the same idealized architecture. While nonnegative recurrence multipliers prevent diagonal SSMs from implementing counting in floating-point arithmetic, unsigned-integer quantization allows arbitrary even counters.

2 Algebraic Preliminaries

We collect the algebraic notions on which the rest of the paper rests. These notions are closely related to automata theory; the interested reader is referred to Pin (2010).

2.1 Alphabets, Words, and Languages

Definition 2.1.

An alphabet is a finite non-empty set Σ\Sigma. The set Σ∗\Sigma^{*} of finite sequences (words) over Σ\Sigma, equipped with concatenation and the empty word ε\varepsilon as identity, is the free monoid on Σ\Sigma.

Definition 2.2.

A language over Σ\Sigma is a subset ℒ⊆Σ∗\mathcal{L}\subseteq\Sigma^{*}. Its characteristic function is

χℒ:Σ∗⟶{0,1},χℒ​(w)={1,w∈ℒ,0,w∉ℒ.\chi_{\mathcal{L}}\colon\Sigma^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\},\qquad\chi_{\mathcal{L}}(w)=\begin{cases}1,&w\in\mathcal{L},\\ 0,&w\notin\mathcal{L}.\end{cases}

We treat recurrent language models as recognizers: their role is to compute χℒ\chi_{\mathcal{L}}, not to define a distribution over Σ∗\Sigma^{*}.

2.2 Monoids

Definition 2.3.

A monoid is a triple (M,⋅,1M)(M,\cdot,1_{M}) where MM is a set, ⋅\cdot is an associative binary operation on MM, and 1M∈M1_{M}\in M satisfies 1M⋅m=m⋅1M=m1_{M}\cdot m=m\cdot 1_{M}=m for all m∈Mm\in M. We usually omit the operation and the identity from the notation and write MM for the monoid.

The free monoid Σ∗\Sigma^{*} is the prototypical example: the identity is the empty word, and concatenation is associative.

Definition 2.4.

A monoid morphism between monoids MM and NN is a map ϕ:M→N\phi\colon M\to N satisfying ϕ⁡(1M)=1N\phi(1_{M})=1_{N} and ϕ⁡(m1⋅m2)=ϕ⁡(m1)⋅ϕ⁡(m2)\phi(m_{1}\cdot m_{2})=\phi(m_{1})\cdot\phi(m_{2}) for all m1,m2∈Mm_{1},m_{2}\in M.

A monoid morphism with domain Σ∗\Sigma^{*} is uniquely determined by its values on letters: any set map ϕ:Σ→N\phi\colon\Sigma\to N extends uniquely to a monoid morphism ϕ^:Σ∗→N\widehat{\phi}\colon\Sigma^{*}\to N.

2.3 Transformation Monoids

Definition 2.5.

For a set QQ, the set QQQ^{Q} of all functions Q→QQ\to Q is a monoid under composition, with identity the identity function idQ\mathrm{id}_{Q}. We call QQQ^{Q} the full transformation monoid of QQ.

Definition 2.6.

A transformation monoid is a pair (M,Q)(M,Q) consisting of a set QQ and a submonoid M≤QQM\leq Q^{Q}. Equivalently, MM is a monoid equipped with a monoid morphism ρ:M→QQ\rho\colon M\to Q^{Q}, called the action, with ρ⁡(1M)=idQ\rho(1_{M})=\mathrm{id}_{Q}. We write m⋅q=defρ​(m)​(q)m\cdot q\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\rho(m)(q) and identify MM with its image ρ⁡(M)\rho(M) when ρ\rho is injective.

2.4 Composition of Transformation Monoids

We will repeatedly compose transformation monoids in two distinct ways: in parallel, modeling components that operate independently, and in cascade, modeling components arranged in a hierarchy where lower layers control the dynamics of upper ones.

Definition 2.7.

Let (M1,Q1),…,(Mn,Qn)(M_{1},Q_{1}),\ldots,(M_{n},Q_{n}) be transformation monoids. Their parallel composition (or direct product) is the transformation monoid (M1×⋯×Mn,Q1×⋯×Qn)(M_{1}\times\cdots\times M_{n},Q_{1}\times\cdots\times Q_{n}) with componentwise action

(m1,…,mn)⋅(q1,…,qn)=def(m1⋅q1,…,mn⋅qn).(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n})\cdot(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}(m_{1}\cdot q_{1},\ldots,m_{n}\cdot q_{n}).

The identity is (idQ1,…,idQn)(\mathrm{id}_{Q_{1}},\ldots,\mathrm{id}_{Q_{n}}).

Definition 2.8.

Let (M1,Q1)(M_{1},Q_{1}) and (M2,Q2)(M_{2},Q_{2}) be transformation monoids. The (left) wreath product (M1,Q1)≀(M2,Q2)(M_{1},Q_{1})\wr(M_{2},Q_{2}) has underlying set M1×M2Q1M_{1}\times M_{2}^{Q_{1}} and state space Q1×Q2Q_{1}\times Q_{2}. Multiplication and action are

(m1,ϕ1)​(m2,ϕ2)\displaystyle(m_{1},\phi_{1})(m_{2},\phi_{2}) =def(m1m2,q1↦ϕ1(m2⋅q1)ϕ2(q1)),\displaystyle\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl(m_{1}m_{2},q_{1}\mapsto\phi_{1}(m_{2}\cdot q_{1})\phi_{2}(q_{1})\bigr),
(m1,ϕ1)​(q1,q2)\displaystyle(m_{1},\phi_{1})(q_{1},q_{2}) =def(m1⋅q1,ϕ1​(q1)⋅q2),\displaystyle\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl(m_{1}\cdot q_{1},\phi_{1}(q_{1})\cdot q_{2}\bigr),

with identity (1M1,q1↦1M2)(1_{M_{1}},q_{1}\mapsto 1_{M_{2}}). The wreath product of monoids is a monoid; of transformation monoids, a transformation monoid.

The wreath product is the algebraic counterpart of cascade composition on the machine side: it captures the structure obtained when two transducers are composed in a hierarchy where the lower one controls the dynamics of the upper.

Remark 2.9 (Left convention).

We adopt the left wreath product, where the upper-layer transition ϕ⁡(q)\phi(q) depends on the old lower-layer state qq. This matches the feedforward dependency in deep recurrent architectures, where the input delivered to layer n+1n+1 at time tt is computed from the state of layer nn as it stands at the beginning of step tt, before layer nn updates on the symbol at time tt. The right wreath convention (more common in classical algebraic automata theory) is obtained by reversing operand order, but the algebraic content is the same.

Remark 2.10 (Associativity up to canonical isomorphism).

The wreath product of transformation monoids is associative up to canonical isomorphism, i.e., the state spaces (Q1×Q2)×Q3(Q_{1}\times Q_{2})\times Q_{3} and Q1×(Q2×Q3)Q_{1}\times(Q_{2}\times Q_{3}) of the two bracketings of (M1,Q1)≀(M2,Q2)≀(M3,Q3)(M_{1},Q_{1})\wr(M_{2},Q_{2})\wr(M_{3},Q_{3}) differ, and the underlying monoids (M1×M2Q1)×M3Q1×Q2(M_{1}\times M_{2}^{Q_{1}})\times M_{3}^{Q_{1}\times Q_{2}} and M1×(M2×M3Q2)Q1M_{1}\times(M_{2}\times M_{3}^{Q_{2}})^{Q_{1}} are identified by re-association and the Curry isomorphism M3Q1×Q2≅(M3Q2)Q1M_{3}^{Q_{1}\times Q_{2}}\cong(M_{3}^{Q_{2}})^{Q_{1}}. We henceforth write iterated wreath products without parentheses, equality between such expressions denoting the canonical isomorphism.

2.5 Division of Monoids

The right notion of “M1M_{1} is structurally simpler than M2M_{2}” is not inclusion but division.

Definition 2.11.

A monoid M1M_{1} divides a monoid M2M_{2}, written M1≺M2M_{1}\prec M_{2}, if M1M_{1} is a quotient of a submonoid of M2M_{2}: there exist a submonoid N≤M2N\leq M_{2} and a surjective monoid morphism π:N↠M1\pi\colon N\twoheadrightarrow M_{1}. Division of transformation monoids is defined analogously, requiring π\pi to be compatible with the actions on the respective state spaces.

Division induces a preorder on monoids. It is the relation that survives the abstraction from concrete dynamics to syntactic monoids: the syntactic monoid of any language recognized by a transducer divides its transition monoid, as recorded in Proposition 2.16.

2.6 Recognition of Languages by Monoids

The link between formal languages and monoids is given by Schützenberger’s (1955) recognition theorem. Our presentation is based on Eilenberg (1976).

Definition 2.12.

A monoid MM recognizes a language ℒ⊆Σ∗\mathcal{L}\subseteq\Sigma^{*} if there exist a monoid morphism η:Σ∗→M\eta\colon\Sigma^{*}\to M and a subset P⊆MP\subseteq M such that ℒ=η−1​(P)\mathcal{L}=\eta^{-1}(P).

Theorem 2.13.

For every language ℒ⊆Σ∗\mathcal{L}\subseteq\Sigma^{*}, there exists a unique-up-to-isomorphism monoid M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}), the syntactic monoid of ℒ\mathcal{L}, characterized by the universal property that for any monoid MM and morphism η:Σ∗→M\eta\colon\Sigma^{*}\to M recognizing ℒ\mathcal{L}, the morphism η\eta factors through a surjective morphism onto M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}). Equivalently, M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) is the quotient of Σ∗\Sigma^{*} by the syntactic congruence

u∼ℒv⇔∀x,y∈Σ∗:xuy∈ℒ⇔xvy∈ℒ.u\sim_{\mathcal{L}}v\iff\forall x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\colon xuy\in\mathcal{L}\Leftrightarrow xvy\in\mathcal{L}.

A language ℒ\mathcal{L} is regular if and only if M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) is finite.

The syntactic monoid is the smallest algebraic object that captures everything a monoid morphism out of Σ∗\Sigma^{*} can know about ℒ\mathcal{L}. Expressivity statements of the form architecture 𝒜\mathcal{A} recognizes language ℒ\mathcal{L} will, in this paper, factor through statements of the form M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) divides the transition monoid of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

2.7 Transducers and Acceptors

A useful intermediate object between a monoid morphism and a finite-state recognizer is the transducer: a state machine that processes a word symbol by symbol, updating an internal state and emitting an output at each step. We use it throughout the paper to model individual layers of a recurrent architecture.

Definition 2.14.

A transducer is a tuple 𝒯=(Q,q∘,X,Y,δ,γ)\mathcal{T}=(Q,q^{\circ},X,Y,\delta,\gamma) where QQ is a state set with initial state q∘∈Qq^{\circ}\in Q, XX is an input set, YY is an output set, δ:Q×X→Q\delta\colon Q\times X\to Q is the transition map, and γ:Q×X→Y\gamma\colon Q\times X\to Y is the output map. Both maps are total.

The transition map δ\delta extends inductively to a map δ^:Q×X∗→Q\widehat{\delta}\colon Q\times X^{*}\to Q on words:

δ^​(q,ε)=q,δ^​(q,w⋅x)=δ⁡(δ^​(q,w),x).\widehat{\delta}(q,\varepsilon)=q,\qquad\widehat{\delta}(q,w\cdot x)=\delta(\widehat{\delta}(q,w),x).

The transducer above is in the Mealy form: the output γ⁡(q,x)\gamma(q,x) depends on both the state and the current letter. When Y={0,1}Y=\{0,1\}, the transducer is an acceptor; the language it recognizes consists of non-empty words w=w′⋅x∈X+w=w^{\prime}\cdot x\in X^{+}, where w′∈X∗w^{\prime}\in X^{*} and x∈Xx\in X, satisfying γ⁡(δ^​(q∘,w′),x)=1\gamma(\widehat{\delta}(q^{\circ},w^{\prime}),x)=1. Whether the empty word ε\varepsilon is accepted requires an additional convention. We resolve this asymmetry in Section 3.6 by adopting a state-only readout for acceptance, where acceptance is a predicate on states and the empty word’s status is determined by the initial state alone. For the Moore variant (output independent of input, γ⁡(q,x)=γ⁡(q)\gamma(q,x)=\gamma(q)), the more familiar formula

ℒ⁡(𝒯)={w∈X∗:δ^​(q∘,w)∈F}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T})=\{w\in X^{*}:\widehat{\delta}(q^{\circ},w)\in F\}

with F=γ−1​(1)⊆QF=\gamma^{-1}(1)\subseteq Q applies, and the empty word is accepted iff q∘∈Fq^{\circ}\in F.

2.8 Transition Monoid of a Transducer

Definition 2.15.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a transducer. For each x∈Xx\in X, the induced transition of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is

δx:Q→Q,q↦δ⁡(q,x).\delta_{x}\colon Q\to Q,\qquad q\mapsto\delta(q,x).

The transition monoid of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is

T𝒯=def⟨δx∣x∈X⟩mon≤QQ,T_{\mathcal{T}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl\langle\delta_{x}\mid x\in X\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\leq Q^{Q},

the submonoid of QQQ^{Q} generated by the induced transitions, together with idQ\mathrm{id}_{Q}.

The transition monoid is the algebraic object that records all state transformations obtainable by feeding finite input words to 𝒯\mathcal{T}, including the empty word.

Proposition 2.16.

If 𝒯\mathcal{T} is an acceptor recognizing ℒ⊆X∗\mathcal{L}\subseteq X^{*}, then the syntactic monoid M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) divides T𝒯T_{\mathcal{T}}:

M⁡(ℒ)≺T𝒯.M(\mathcal{L})\prec T_{\mathcal{T}}.

This is the connection between the dynamical view (monoid of transformations of states) and the language view (syntactic monoid) that the rest of the paper exploits.

3 Algebraic RNNs

Recurrent language models, in their analytic form, are typically defined in terms of real-valued tensors, smooth nonlinearities, and parameter matrices. The paper strips this down to the structure that survives discretization: a typed family of total maps and their iterated composition, specified combinatorially before any choice of arithmetic semantics. The arithmetic then enters as a parameter, fixing the concrete sets and transition functions each algebraic core realizes.

3.1 Algebraic Cores

Definition 3.1.

An algebraic core is a tuple 𝔠=(Q,X,Y,f,g)\mathfrak{c}=(Q,X,Y,f,g) where QQ, XX, and YY are sets, and

f\displaystyle f :Q×X→Q,\displaystyle\colon Q\times X\to Q, g\displaystyle g :Q×X→Y\displaystyle\colon Q\times X\to Y

are total maps, called respectively the transition and readout functions.

Mealy, not Moore.

When QQ, XX, YY are finite, 𝔠\mathfrak{c} is precisely a Mealy machine (Mealy, 1955), the standard finite-state transducer of classical automata theory (Eilenberg, 1976). The fact that gg depends on both the state and the current letter–not on the state alone–distinguishes Mealy machines from their Moore counterparts (Moore, 1956). We retain this Mealy-style readout (depending on both state and input) because the recurrent layers we wish to abstract (e.g., Elman, SSM) all share it.

Definition 3.2.

Let 𝔠\mathfrak{c} be an algebraic core. For each x∈Xx\in X, the induced transition is

fx:Q→Q,q↦f⁡(q,x).f_{x}\colon Q\to Q,\qquad q\mapsto f(q,x).

The transition monoid of 𝔠\mathfrak{c} is the submonoid of QQQ^{Q} generated by these maps,

M𝔠=def⟨fx∣x∈X⟩mon≤QQ,M_{\mathfrak{c}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl\langle f_{x}\mid x\in X\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\leq Q^{Q},

and the pair (M𝔠,Q)(M_{\mathfrak{c}},Q) is the associated transformation monoid.

Remark 3.3 (Dynamics versus observability).

The readout gg contributes nothing to M𝔠M_{\mathfrak{c}}. The monoid encodes the dynamics reachable on QQ; the readout encodes observability. This separation will matter: the same dynamical core can support distinct readouts, and a given language is recognized by a quotient of the dynamics determined by its observable consequences. We return to this point in Section 3.6.

3.2 Algebraic RNNs

Definition 3.4.

An algebraic RNN of depth NN is a tuple

ℛ=(𝔠1,(𝔠2,τ1),…,(𝔠N,τN−1)),\mathcal{R}=\bigl(\mathfrak{c}_{1},(\mathfrak{c}_{2},\tau_{1}),\ldots,(\mathfrak{c}_{N},\tau_{N-1})\bigr),

where each 𝔠n=(Qn,Xn,Yn,fn,gn)\mathfrak{c}_{n}=(Q_{n},X_{n},Y_{n},f_{n},g_{n}) is an algebraic core, and each τn−1:Xn−1×Yn−1→Xn\tau_{n-1}\colon X_{n-1}\times Y_{n-1}\to X_{n} for 2≤n≤N2\leq n\leq N is a wiring map from 𝔠n−1\mathfrak{c}_{n-1} to 𝔠n\mathfrak{c}_{n}. The first core has no incoming wiring. The global state space of ℛ\mathcal{R} is

Qℛ=defQ1×⋯×QN.Q_{\mathcal{R}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}Q_{1}\times\cdots\times Q_{N}.

The input type of ℛ\mathcal{R} is the set In⁡(ℛ)=defX1\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}X_{1}, and the output type of ℛ\mathcal{R} is the pair Out⁡(ℛ)=def(XN,YN)\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}(X_{N},Y_{N}).

The asymmetry between the two reflects the type-signature of wiring maps, which consume a pair X×YX\times Y to produce an input. The pair (In⁡(ℛ),Out⁡(ℛ))(\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}),\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R})) records precisely the external interface of ℛ\mathcal{R}.

An algebraic RNN is, on its own, neither an acceptor nor a generator: it is best viewed as a transducer. The two further pieces of structure needed to turn it into a language acceptor (an initial state, an encoder, an accepting core) are deferred to Section 3.6. Before adding them, we identify the algebraic object inside which ℛ\mathcal{R} already lives.

3.3 Cascade Juxtaposition

The construction of an algebraic RNN by appending a new core to a cascade, as an accepting core, an initialization core, or a post-processing core, appears repeatedly throughout this paper. We give the operation a formal name and observe that, with input and output types separated, it becomes the associative composition of a typed category.

Wirings as type morphisms.

Given an algebraic RNN ℛ\mathcal{R} with output type Out⁡(ℛ)=(XN,YN)\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R})=(X_{N},Y_{N}) and an algebraic RNN ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} with input type In⁡(ℛ′)=X1′\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime})=X_{1}^{\prime}, a wiring map from ℛ\mathcal{R} to ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} is a function

τ:Out⁡(ℛ)⟶In⁡(ℛ′),\tau\colon\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R})\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}),

i.e., a map XN×YN→X1′X_{N}\times Y_{N}\to X_{1}^{\prime}. The output type of ℛ\mathcal{R} and the input type of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} thus carry all the information needed to specify τ\tau’s domain and codomain.

Definition 3.5.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} be algebraic RNNs of depths NN and N′N^{\prime}, and let τ:Out⁡(ℛ)→In⁡(ℛ′)\tau\colon\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R})\to\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}) be a wiring map between them. The cascade juxtaposition of ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} along τ\tau is the algebraic RNN of depth N+N′N+N^{\prime} obtained by concatenating their sequences of pairs:

ℛ⊳τℛ′=def(𝔠1,…,(𝔠N,τN−1),(𝔠1′,τ),…,(𝔠N′′,τN′−1′))\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\dots,(\mathfrak{c}_{N},\tau_{N-1}),(\mathfrak{c}_{1}^{\prime},\tau),\dots,(\mathfrak{c}_{N^{\prime}}^{\prime},\tau_{N^{\prime}-1}^{\prime}))

where the wiring of the first core of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} is taken to be τ\tau. The juxtaposition has input type In⁡(ℛ)\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}) and output type Out⁡(ℛ′)\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}):

In⁡(ℛ⊳τℛ′)=In⁡(ℛ),Out⁡(ℛ⊳τℛ′)=Out⁡(ℛ′).\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime})=\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}),\qquad\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime})=\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}).

The special case where ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} is the depth-one RNN with a single pair (𝔠′,τ)(\mathfrak{c}^{\prime},\tau) recovers the operation of appending a single core to a cascade.

Remark 3.6.

Cascade juxtaposition is associative, once input and output types are tracked. Given three algebraic RNNs ℛ1,ℛ2,ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{1},\mathcal{R}_{2},\mathcal{R}_{3} and wiring maps τ12:Out⁡(ℛ1)→In⁡(ℛ2)\tau_{12}\colon\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R}_{1})\to\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}_{2}), τ23:Out⁡(ℛ2)→In⁡(ℛ3)\tau_{23}\colon\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R}_{2})\to\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}_{3}), the type of τ23\tau_{23} depends only on Out⁡(ℛ2)\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R}_{2}) and In⁡(ℛ3)\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}_{3}), both unchanged by either parenthesization. The two expressions (ℛ1⊳τ12ℛ2)⊳τ23ℛ3(\mathcal{R}_{1}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{12}}}\mathcal{R}_{2})\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{23}}}\mathcal{R}_{3} and ℛ1⊳τ12(ℛ2⊳τ23ℛ3)\mathcal{R}_{1}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{12}}}(\mathcal{R}_{2}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{23}}}\mathcal{R}_{3}) produce the same sequence of pairs (𝔠n,τn−1)(\mathfrak{c}_{n},\tau_{n-1}) and hence, by Definition 3.4, denote the same algebraic RNN. Iterated juxtaposition 𝔠1⊳τ2𝔠2⊳τ3⋯⊳τN𝔠N\mathfrak{c}_{1}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{2}}}\mathfrak{c}_{2}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{3}}}\cdots\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{N}}}\mathfrak{c}_{N} is therefore well-defined once the typed sequence of cores and wirings is fixed.

Remark 3.7 (General wirings).

The wiring maps of Definition 3.4 are local: each τn\tau_{n} depends only on the input and output of the immediately preceding core 𝔠n−1\mathfrak{c}_{n-1}. This convention is sufficient to model the standard recurrent architectures.

The framework extends, however, to general wirings

τn:X≤n−1×Y≤n−1→Xn,\tau_{n}\colon X_{\leq n-1}\times Y_{\leq n-1}\to X_{n},

where X≤n−1=defX1×⋯×Xn−1X_{\leq n-1}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}X_{1}\times\cdots\times X_{n-1} and similarly for Y≤n−1Y_{\leq n-1}. Such wirings give layer nn direct access to the inputs and outputs of all preceding layers, modeling arbitrary skip connections, dense connections, and residual shortcuts that bypass intermediate layers.

The transition to general wirings affects only one definition in the body of the paper. The layer-input dependency map (Definition 3.9) acquires the corresponding extended recursion: writing xn=φnT​(q<n,t)x_{n}=\varphi_{n}^{T}(q_{<n},t) and yn=gn​(fn​(qn,xn),xn)y_{n}=g_{n}(f_{n}(q_{n},x_{n}),x_{n}),

φn+1T​(q<n+1,t)=defτn​((x1,…,xn),(y1,…,yn)).\varphi_{n+1}^{T}(q_{<n+1},t)\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\tau_{n}\bigl((x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\bigr).

Every other algebraic statement of the paper passes through verbatim. The factorization lemma (Lemma 3.12) still holds: the induction on depth uses only that the input to layer n+1n+1 is determined by (q<n+1,t)(q_{<n+1},t), which the general wiring respects. The cascade juxtaposition identity (Proposition 3.20) remains valid: the projection π≤N\pi_{\leq N} is still surjective onto the dynamics of the lower segment. The syntactic divisibility chain leading to M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))≺Wℛ+e⁡(Σ)M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}))\prec W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)} holds as before.

The price of generality is notational. Under general wirings, the output type of ℛ\mathcal{R} inflates from the pair (XN,YN)(X_{N},Y_{N}) to the full history (X≤N,Y≤N)(X_{\leq N},Y_{\leq N}). Cascade juxtaposition ℛ⊳τℛ′\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime} then takes a wiring τ:X≤N×Y≤N→X1′\tau\colon X_{\leq N}\times Y_{\leq N}\to X_{1}^{\prime}, and the typed associativity of Remark 3.6 holds modulo this enriched type accounting.

We adopt the local form throughout for notational simplicity, with the understanding that none of the algebraic results of the paper are specific to it.

3.4 The Ambient Wreath Product

Write Mn=defM𝔠nM_{n}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}M_{\mathfrak{c}_{n}} for the transition monoid of the nthn^{\text{th}} core, and (Mn,Qn)(M_{n},Q_{n}) for its transformation monoid.

Definition 3.8.

The ambient wreath product of ℛ\mathcal{R} is the iterated transformation monoid

𝕎1=def(M1,Q1),𝕎n+1=def𝕎n≀(Mn+1,Qn+1).\mathbb{W}_{1}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}(M_{1},Q_{1}),\qquad\mathbb{W}_{n+1}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\mathbb{W}_{n}\wr(M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}).

We write 𝕎ℛ=def𝕎N=(Wℛ,Qℛ)\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\mathbb{W}_{N}=(W_{\mathcal{R}},Q_{\mathcal{R}}). By construction, (Wℛ,Qℛ)≤(QℛQℛ,Qℛ)(W_{\mathcal{R}},Q_{\mathcal{R}})\leq(Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{Q_{\mathcal{R}}},Q_{\mathcal{R}}) is a transformation monoid on the global state space.

The ambient wreath product of ℛ\mathcal{R} captures all cores and their hierarchical dependency, but is blind to the wiring maps τn\tau_{n}. Every layer nn may, in 𝕎ℛ\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}, be driven by any input in XnX_{n}, regardless of which inputs the wiring actually activates. The realized dynamics live in a strictly smaller sub-object.

3.5 Realized Dynamics: a Parameterized Construction

We now refine 𝕎ℛ\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}} to a sub-transformation-monoid that respects the wiring. We parameterize the construction by an arbitrary set T⊆X1T\subseteq X_{1} of admissible inputs to the first core, prove a single factorization lemma at this level of generality, and recover the two cases of interest (the unconstrained RNN and the RNN as language acceptor) as specializations.

Definition 3.9.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be an algebraic RNN of depth NN and let T⊆X1T\subseteq X_{1}. The layer-input dependency maps of ℛ\mathcal{R} relative to TT, denoted φnT\varphi_{n}^{T}, are defined as follows

φnT:Q<n×T→Xn,Q<n=defQ1×⋯×Qn−1\varphi_{n}^{T}\colon Q_{<n}\times T\to X_{n},\quad Q_{<n}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}Q_{1}\times\cdots\times Q_{n-1}

(with Q<1Q_{<1} a singleton, so that φ1T\varphi_{1}^{T} is essentially the map T→X1,t↦tT\to X_{1},t\mapsto t) are defined inductively: For 1<n≤N1<n\leq N, writing xn=φnT​(q<n,t)x_{n}=\varphi_{n}^{T}(q_{<n},t),

φn+1T​(q<n+1,t)=defτn−1​(xn,gn​(fn​(qn,xn),xn)).\displaystyle\varphi_{n+1}^{T}(q_{<n+1},t)\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\tau_{n-1}\Bigl(x_{n},g_{n}\bigl(f_{n}(q_{n},x_{n}),x_{n}\bigr)\Bigr).

The reachable input set11 1 Sometimes called the effective or realized input set in the literature; we use reachable to emphasize that this set is the image of the layer-input dependency map starting from TT. at layer nn is XnT=defIm⁡(φnT)⊆XnX_{n}^{T}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\mathrm{Im}(\varphi_{n}^{T})\subseteq X_{n}.

The set XnTX_{n}^{T} is the set of inputs that the wiring can actually deliver to layer nn when the first core is driven by letters from TT.

Definition 3.10.

The realized transition monoid of layer nn relative to TT is

MnT=def⟨(fn)x∣x∈XnT⟩mon≤Mn.M_{n}^{T}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl\langle(f_{n})_{x}\mid x\in X_{n}^{T}\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\leq M_{n}.
Definition 3.11.

The realized wreath product of ℛ\mathcal{R} relative to TT is

𝕎ℛT=def(M1T,Q1)≀⋯≀(MNT,QN)≤𝕎ℛ,\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}(M_{1}^{T},Q_{1})\wr\cdots\wr(M_{N}^{T},Q_{N})\leq\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}},

with underlying monoid WℛTW_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}.

Lemma 3.12 (Factorization).

Let T⊆X1T\subseteq X_{1}. For each t∈Tt\in T, the global state update

(Fℛ)t:Qℛ→Qℛ(F_{\mathcal{R}})_{t}\colon Q_{\mathcal{R}}\to Q_{\mathcal{R}}

induced by feeding tt into the first core is an element of WℛTW_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}. Consequently, the global transition monoid driven by TT,

MℛT=def⟨(Fℛ)t∣t∈T⟩mon,M_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl\langle(F_{\mathcal{R}})_{t}\mid t\in T\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}},

satisfies

MℛT≤WℛT≤Wℛ.M_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\leq W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\leq W_{\mathcal{R}}.
Proof sketch.

Induction on NN, as in Appendix E. The base case is immediate. For the inductive step, the global update splits as (Fℛ)t​(q,qN)=(F¯​(q),ψF¯,t​(q)​(qN))(F_{\mathcal{R}})_{t}(q,q_{N})=(\bar{F}(q),\psi_{\bar{F},t}(q)(q_{N})) for q∈Q<N+1q\in Q_{<N+1}, where F¯∈Wℛ|<NT\bar{F}\in W_{\mathcal{R}|_{<N}}^{T} by induction and ψF¯,t​(q)=(fN)φNT​(q,t)∈MNT\psi_{\bar{F},t}(q)=(f_{N})_{\varphi_{N}^{T}(q,t)}\in M_{N}^{T} by Definition 3.10. This is precisely the action of an element of the wreath product. The action of the empty word in T∗T^{*} corresponds to idQℛ∈WℛT\mathrm{id}_{Q_{\mathcal{R}}}\in W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}. ∎

Remark 3.13 (Functoriality in TT).

The assignment T↦𝕎ℛTT\mapsto\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{T} is a covariant functor from the poset (𝒫⁡(X1),⊆)(\mathcal{P}(X_{1}),\subseteq) to the poset of transformation submonoids of 𝕎ℛ\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}, ordered by inclusion (see Remark E.1). Explicitly: if T⊆T′T\subseteq T^{\prime}, then XnT⊆XnT′X_{n}^{T}\subseteq X_{n}^{T^{\prime}} at every layer, hence MnT≤MnT′M_{n}^{T}\leq M_{n}^{T^{\prime}} and 𝕎ℛT≤𝕎ℛT′\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\leq\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{T^{\prime}}. The ambient case is the terminal value: 𝕎ℛX1=𝕎ℛ\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{X_{1}}=\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}.

Two specializations of Lemma 3.12 are of primary interest. The terminal case T=X1T=X_{1} recovers the ambient wreath product (𝕎ℛX1=𝕎ℛ\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{X_{1}}=\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}, by Remark 3.13) and is the relevant setting when ℛ\mathcal{R} is viewed as an autonomous transducer freely driven by inputs to its first core. The case T=e⁡(Σ)T=e(\Sigma), for some encoder e:Σ→X1e\colon\Sigma\to X_{1} of a finite alphabet Σ\Sigma, is the relevant setting when ℛ\mathcal{R} is the dynamical backbone of a language acceptor (Section 3.6): the realized wreath product 𝕎ℛe⁡(Σ)\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{e(\Sigma)} then governs the dynamics reachable by feeding Σ∗\Sigma^{*} into ℛ\mathcal{R}, and divides the recognized language’s algebra.

3.6 Algebraic RNNs as Language Acceptors

3.6.1 Accepting core

A classical automaton accepts via a final-state set F⊆QF\subseteq Q. The algebraic RNNs of Definition 3.4 carry instead, in their last core, a Mealy-style readout gN:QN×XN→YNg_{N}\colon Q_{N}\times X_{N}\to Y_{N} whose value depends jointly on the post-update state and the last input read. Composing with a decoder d:YN→{0,1}d\colon Y_{N}\to\{0,1\} thus yields not a subset of QNQ_{N} but a subset of QN×XNQ_{N}\times X_{N}. The acceptance condition becomes a predicate on (state, last symbol) pairs rather than on states alone, and the algebraic recognition framework of Eilenberg (1976) does not apply directly.

We resolve this not by external bookkeeping, as would be done by reserving a dedicated end-of-sequence symbol, but structurally, by absorbing the decoder into the algebra itself. The decoder dd is realized as an additional algebraic core, appended to the architecture, whose internal state evolves under the same wiring discipline as every other layer and whose role is to contain the acceptance condition as a property of its own state.

Definition 3.14.

An accepting core is an algebraic core 𝔠∙=(Q∙,X∙,{0,1},f∙,g∙){\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}=(Q_{\bullet},X_{\bullet},\{0,1\},f_{\bullet},g_{\bullet}) whose readout depends only on the state: there exists a subset F⊆Q∙F\subseteq Q_{\bullet}, called the accepting region, such that

g∙​(q,x)=χF​(q)for all ​q∈Q∙,x∈X∙,g_{\bullet}(q,x)=\chi_{F}(q)\quad\text{for all }q\in Q_{\bullet},\ x\in X_{\bullet},

where χF:Q∙→{0,1}\chi_{F}\colon Q_{\bullet}\to\{0,1\} is the characteristic function of FF.

Remark 3.15 (Moore content).

Definition 3.14 captures, in algebraic terms, exactly the structure of a Moore machine with Boolean output: the readout depends only on the state, which is what turns acceptance into a predicate on states rather than a predicate on state-letter pairs. When Q∙Q_{\bullet} is a singleton, 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} degenerates to a pure set map X∙→{0,1}X_{\bullet}\to\{0,1\}, recovering the memoryless decoder d:YN→{0,1}d\colon Y_{N}\to\{0,1\} of the literature (precomposed with the wiring map). The present formulation thus strictly generalizes that one: it allows the decoder to be itself stateful, while specializing back to a memoryless decision in the singleton case.

3.6.2 RNN acceptors

Definition 3.16.

An RNN acceptor is a tuple 𝒜=(Σ,ℛ+,q∘,e)\mathcal{A}=(\Sigma,{\mathcal{R}^{+}},q^{\circ},e) where where ℛ+=ℛ⊳τN𝔠∙{\mathcal{R}^{+}}=\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{N}}}{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} is the augmented RNN obtained by appending an accepting core 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} to a base RNN ℛ\mathcal{R} via a wiring map τN\tau_{N}, and:

  • •

    Σ\Sigma is a finite alphabet;

  • •

    ℛ\mathcal{R} is an algebraic RNN of depth NN, which we name the base RNN of 𝒜\mathcal{A};

  • •

    𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} is an accepting core (Definition 3.14);

  • •

    τN:XN×YN→X∙\tau_{N}\colon X_{N}\times Y_{N}\to X_{\bullet} is the wiring map between ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}};

  • •

    q∘∈Qℛ+q^{\circ}\in Q_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} is an initial global state;

  • •

    e:Σ→X1e\colon\Sigma\to X_{1} is the encoder.

The wiring map is, in every case, part of the acceptor’s specification.

Remark 3.17 (The role of ℛ+{\mathcal{R}^{+}}).

The augmented RNN ℛ+{\mathcal{R}^{+}} is, by Definition 3.4, a genuine algebraic RNN: the Moore constraint on 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} acts only at the last layer and does not affect the application of the algebraic theory of Section 3.5 to ℛ+{\mathcal{R}^{+}}.

Remark 3.18 (The acceptor as a sandwich).

The definition of an RNN acceptor (Definition 3.16) treats q∘q^{\circ} and FF asymmetrically: the initial state q∘q^{\circ} enters as direct primitive data, while the accepting region FF is wrapped inside the accepting core 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} as part of its algebraic structure. This asymmetry is dispensable. Indeed, the initial state, like the accepting core, can be internalized into an algebraic core as well, placed at the input end of the cascade. Concretely, an initialization core is an algebraic core 𝔠∘=(Q∘,X∘,Y∘,f∘,g∘){\mathfrak{c}_{\circ}}=(Q_{\circ},X_{\circ},Y_{\circ},f_{\circ},g_{\circ}) equipped with a distinguished input σ∗∈X∘\sigma_{*}\in X_{\circ} and a base state q∘0∈Q∘q_{\circ}^{0}\in Q_{\circ}, such that f∘​(q∘0,σ∗)f_{\circ}(q_{\circ}^{0},\sigma_{*}) delivers, via an outgoing wiring map, the desired initial state q∘q^{\circ} to the next core, and such that f∘​(q,x)=qf_{\circ}(q,x)=q for all q≠q∘0q\neq q_{\circ}^{0} and all x∈X∘x\in X_{\circ}. The dualized acceptor

𝒜∘=(Σ∪{σ∗},𝔠∘⊳τ0ℛ⊳τN𝔠∙,q∘0,e∘),\mathcal{A}^{\circ}=\bigl(\Sigma\cup\{\sigma_{*}\},{\mathfrak{c}_{\circ}}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{0}}}\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{N}}}{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}},q_{\circ}^{0},e^{\circ}\bigr),

where σ∗∉Σ\sigma_{*}\notin\Sigma is a distinguished prefix symbol, is constructed by juxtaposing 𝔠∘{\mathfrak{c}_{\circ}} to the left of ℛ\mathcal{R} via τ0\tau_{0}, and reading σ∗⋅w\sigma_{*}\cdot w in place of ww. It recognizes exactly ℒ⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}), with identical syntactic monoid M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜∘))=M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\circ}))=M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})). A general acceptor is thus, in its most symmetric form, a sandwich

𝔠∘⊳τ0ℛ⊳τN𝔠∙,{\mathfrak{c}_{\circ}}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{0}}}\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{N}}}{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}},

with an initialization core 𝔠∘{\mathfrak{c}_{\circ}} at the input end of the cascade and an accepting core 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} at the output end. The initialization core contributes a one-element submonoid to the realized wreath product (the identity, after its first action), so divisibility arguments collapse its contribution to triviality: the dualization is harmless at the level of recognized languages and their syntactic monoids. We do not adopt the dualized form as a working definition. The standard formulation (Definition 3.16) is closer to the machine-learning idiom in which an RNN’s initial state is part of its specification.

3.6.3 Algebraic content

Definition 3.19.

Let 𝒜=(Σ,ℛ+,q∘,e)\mathcal{A}=(\Sigma,{\mathcal{R}^{+}},q^{\circ},e) be an RNN acceptor. For w=σ1⋯σn∈Σ∗w=\sigma_{1}\cdots\sigma_{n}\in\Sigma^{*}, write F^ℛ+​(q∘,w)∈Qℛ+\widehat{F}_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}(q^{\circ},w)\in Q_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} for the global state obtained by iterating ℛ+{\mathcal{R}^{+}} from q∘q^{\circ} on the encoded sequence e⁡(σ1),…,e⁡(σn)e(\sigma_{1}),\ldots,e(\sigma_{n}), with the convention that the empty word acts as idQℛ+\mathrm{id}_{Q_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}}, so that in particular F^ℛ+​(q∘,ε)=q∘\widehat{F}_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}(q^{\circ},\varepsilon)=q^{\circ}. The language recognized by 𝒜\mathcal{A} is

ℒ⁡(𝒜)=def{w∈Σ∗|πN+1​(F^ℛ+​(q∘,w))∈F},\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\Bigl\{w\in\Sigma^{*}\Bigm|\pi_{N+1}\!\bigl(\widehat{F}_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}(q^{\circ},w)\bigr)\in F\Bigr\},

where πN+1:Qℛ+→QN+1\pi_{N+1}\colon Q_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}\to Q_{N+1} is the projection onto the accepting core’s state coordinate.

The dynamics relevant for ℒ⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}) live in the realized wreath product 𝕎ℛ+e⁡(Σ)\mathbb{W}_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)} associated with the augmented network and the admissible-input set T=e⁡(Σ)⊆X1T=e(\Sigma)\subseteq X_{1}. The encoder lifts to a monoid morphism

Φ𝒜:Σ∗⟶Mℛ+e⁡(Σ),w↦F^ℛ+​(−,w),\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\Sigma^{*}\longrightarrow M_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)},\quad w\mapsto\widehat{F}_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}(-,w),

and

ℒ⁡(𝒜)=Φ𝒜−1​(PF),\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})=\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}^{-1}(P_{F}),

where PF=def{m∈Mℛ+e⁡(Σ):πN+1​(m⋅q∘)∈F}P_{F}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\{m\in M_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)}:\pi_{N+1}(m\cdot q^{\circ})\in F\}. The syntactic monoid M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) therefore divides Mℛ+e⁡(Σ)M_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)}, and by Lemma 3.12 divides the realized wreath product Wℛ+e⁡(Σ)W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)}, which in turn divides the ambient wreath product Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}:

M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))≺Mℛ+e⁡(Σ)≤Wℛ+e⁡(Σ)≤Wℛ+.M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}))\prec M_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)}\leq W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)}\leq W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}. (3.1)
Decomposition of the recognition problem.

The divisibility chain above turns the recognition question into a question about finite monoids. Fix a family of algebraic RNNs, a choice of permissible cores, wirings, and arithmetic semantics fixed once and for all, and a target language ℒ⊆Σ∗\mathcal{L}\subseteq\Sigma^{*}. The question does some acceptor in the family recognize ℒ\mathcal{L}? decomposes as follows:

  1. (i)

    Algebraic impossibility. The syntactic monoid M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) must divide some realized wreath product Wℛ+e⁡(Σ)W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{e(\Sigma)} achievable in the family. Krohn–Rhodes theory (Appendix I) decomposes M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) into flip-flops and prime transformation groups. If any required factor cannot be realized as a layer monoid permitted in the family, no acceptor in the family recognizes ℒ\mathcal{L}.

  2. (ii)

    Observational realization. Conversely, to exhibit a recognizer, one constructs cores realizing the Krohn–Rhodes factors of M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}), wires them so that the realized wreath product contains M⁡(ℒ)M(\mathcal{L}) as a divisor, and chooses the accepting region FF to separate the syntactic congruence classes through the readout-induced quotient.

This decomposition applies uniformly to any architecture family fitting Definition 3.4 under any arithmetic semantics fixed as in Section 4. The case study of Appendix J carries out both directions on diagonal SSMs: the algebraic side rules out modular counting under floating-point recurrences, while the observational side constructs an explicit acceptor for parity under unsigned-integer quantization.

3.6.4 The Augmentation as a Wreath Extension

The cascade juxtaposition ℛ⊳τN𝔠∙\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{N}}}{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} of Definition 3.16 takes a base RNN ℛ\mathcal{R} and an accepting core 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}, glues them by a wiring map τN\tau_{N}, and produces a deeper algebraic RNN. At the level of realized dynamics, the cascade juxtaposition becomes a wreath product: the realized monoid of the augmented RNN sits inside the wreath product of the realized monoid of ℛ\mathcal{R} and the realized monoid of 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}. This sharpens Lemma 3.12 for the acceptor case and isolates the algebraic role of the accepting core.

Proposition 3.20.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} be algebraic RNNs of depths NN and N′N^{\prime} respectively, and let τ:Out⁡(ℛ)→In⁡(ℛ′)\tau\colon\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{R})\to\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}) be a wiring map between them. For any T⊆In⁡(ℛ)T\subseteq\mathrm{In}(\mathcal{R}),

𝕎ℛ⊳τℛ′T=𝕎ℛT≀𝕎ℛ′T,\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T}=\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\wr\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T},

where the equality is understood up to canonical isomorphism (Remark 2.10), and 𝕎ℛ′T\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T} denotes the realized wreath product of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} relative to the set of inputs reachable through τ\tau from states of ℛ\mathcal{R} activated by TT. The realized transition monoid of the juxtaposition satisfies the chain

MℛT≺Mℛ⊳τℛ′T≤WℛT≀Wℛ′T,M_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\prec M_{\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T}\leq W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\wr W_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T},

the first division being given by the canonical projection π≤N:Qℛ⊳τℛ′→Qℛ\pi_{\leq N}\colon Q_{\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}\to Q_{\mathcal{R}}.

Proof.

See Appendix F. ∎

Corollary 3.21 (Augmentation of an acceptor).

Let 𝒜=(Σ,ℛ+,q∘,e)\mathcal{A}=\bigl(\Sigma,{\mathcal{R}^{+}},q^{\circ},e\bigr) be an RNN acceptor with base RNN ℛ\mathcal{R} of depth NN, accepting core 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} and wiring map τN\tau_{N}, and let T=e⁡(Σ)⊆X1T=e(\Sigma)\subseteq X_{1}. Then

Wℛ+T=WℛT≀M𝔠∙T,W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{T}=W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\wr M_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}^{T},

again up to canonical isomorphism, and the chain

MℛT≺Mℛ+T≤WℛT≀M𝔠∙TM_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\prec M_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}^{T}\leq W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\wr M_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}^{T}

holds, with M𝔠∙T≤M𝔠∙M_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}^{T}\leq M_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} the realized transition monoid of 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} relative to the inputs it receives through τN\tau_{N}.

Proof.

Specialization of Proposition 3.20 to the case where ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} is the depth-one RNN consisting of 𝔠∙{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}} alone; the realized wreath product Wℛ′TW_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T} then reduces to M𝔠∙TM_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}^{T}. ∎

Remark 3.22 (The accepting core sits above the dynamics).

Corollary 3.21 makes explicit the following: the augmentation by an accepting core adds expressive resolution above the base RNN without modifying the dynamics on QℛQ_{\mathcal{R}}. For divisibility-based expressivity arguments, the consequence is: M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) divides the augmented monoid Mℛ⊳τN𝔠∙TM_{\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau_{N}}}{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}}^{T}, but not necessarily the base monoid MℛTM_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}. The accepting core may, in general, extract recognition power that the base alone cannot encode, exactly when its own state space Q∙Q_{\bullet} has cardinality greater than one. The interest of the accepting-core formulation, compared to a memoryless decoder, depends on the cardinality of Q∙Q_{\bullet}:

  1. (i)

    If |Q∙|=1|Q_{\bullet}|=1, then M𝔠∙={idQ∙}M_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}=\{\mathrm{id}_{Q_{\bullet}}\} and the wreath extension collapses, WℛT≀M𝔠∙T≅WℛTW_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\wr M_{\mathfrak{c}_{\bullet}}^{T}\cong W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}. The acceptor reduces to a pair (ℛ,F⊆YN)(\mathcal{R},F\subseteq Y_{N}) where FF is a Boolean subset of the base RNN’s last readout values. This yields the formulation of a recognizer found in the literature.

  2. (ii)

    When |Q∙|>1|Q_{\bullet}|>1, the accepting core carries stateful memory above the base dynamics and may extract regular languages that the memoryless case cannot reach.

4 The Impact of Discretization

4.1 Algebraic Properties of Finite-Precision Semantics

Digital computers store numbers in discrete, finite data types. They therefore cannot represent arbitrary real values. Instead, computation is carried out over a finite representable set fp⊆ℝ\textsc{fp}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, and the result of each arithmetic operation is mapped back into fp by rounding or truncation.

For formal expressivity analysis, reasoning over ℝ\mathbb{R} while treating finite precision as a small approximation error fails: quantization alters the very algebraic structure on which expressivity statements rest.

Definition 4.1 (Evaluation tree).

An evaluation tree over a set of binary operations 𝒪\mathcal{O} in kk variables is a finite rooted ordered binary tree whose leaves are labeled by variables x1,…,xkx_{1},\ldots,x_{k} or by constants, and whose internal nodes are labeled by operations in 𝒪\mathcal{O}. A tree thus encodes a parenthesized expression.

Definition 4.2.

An arithmetic model is a triple 𝔐=(𝒟,𝒪,□)\mathfrak{M}=(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{O},\square) with 𝒟\mathcal{D} a value domain in an ambient set (usually ℝ\mathbb{R}), 𝒪\mathcal{O} a finite set of binary operations on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and □\square a rounding map from the ambient set into 𝒟\mathcal{D}. For an evaluation tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} over 𝒪\mathcal{O} with constants in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the evaluation under 𝔐\mathfrak{M} is the function ⟦𝒯⟧𝔐:𝒟k→𝒟\llbracket\mathcal{T}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\colon\mathcal{D}^{k}\to\mathcal{D} defined by induction: at a variable leaf xjx_{j}, ⟦𝒯⟧𝔐=defπj\llbracket\mathcal{T}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\pi_{j} (the jj-th projection); at a constant leaf cc, ⟦𝒯⟧𝔐=defc\llbracket\mathcal{T}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}c; at an internal node 𝒯=𝒯1⊙𝒯2\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}_{1}\odot\mathcal{T}_{2}, ⟦𝒯⟧𝔐=def□⁡(⟦𝒯1⟧𝔐⊙⟦𝒯2⟧𝔐)\llbracket\mathcal{T}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\square\!\bigl(\llbracket\mathcal{T}_{1}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\odot\llbracket\mathcal{T}_{2}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\bigr). An expression ff admits, in general, several evaluation trees; the abbreviation ⟦f⟧𝔐=def⟦𝒯⟧𝔐\llbracket f\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\llbracket\mathcal{T}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}} is used when one such tree is fixed by context.

The dominant arithmetic model in practice is floating-point: a basic operation ⊙∈{+,−,×,÷}\odot\in\{+,-,\times,\div\} is evaluated in real arithmetic and rounded back into fp, yielding a relative error δ\delta with □⁡(a⊙b)=(a⊙b)​(1+δ)\square(a\odot b)=(a\odot b)(1+\delta).

This step breaks associativity. For instance, in IEEE 32-bit floating point, with a=1a=1, b=224b=2^{24}, c=−224c=-2^{24}, and □⁡(1+224)=224\square(1+2^{24})=2^{24}:

(a+b)+c=0≠1=a+(b+c).(a+b)+c=0\neq 1=a+(b+c).

Similar phenomena arise from overflow and exceptional values (see Appendix G). In particular, once associativity is lost, the arithmetic no longer forms a monoid under ⊙\odot, meaning that operations that assume this structure (changing parenthesation of evaluations, etc.) are no longer well-defined.

For an overview of arithmetic models used in the expressivity literature, see Appendix G.

4.2 Evaluation Order

Non-associativity makes evaluation order semantically relevant: the value of an expression may depend on how it is parenthesized. Any expression built from binary operations induces an evaluation tree specifying a bracketing (and, operationally, an order of intermediate rounding).

In algebraic language theory, letter-by-letter transitions are modeled by function composition, which is associative by definition. To treat an RNN update as a monoid operation when the underlying arithmetic is non-associative, two conditions are required:

  1. 1.

    The evaluation order within each transition update must be fixed so that the update map is well-defined on every admissible input.

  2. 2.

    The evaluation of recurrent updates must respect temporal order: the update at time tt must be completed before the update at time t+1t+1.

Definition 4.3 (Recurrence-consistent evaluation).

An evaluation strategy is recurrence-consistent if conditions 1 and 2 are met.

If either condition fails, the model’s behavior on sequences is not a well-defined recurrence, and formal statements about languages recognized via recurrent transitions become ill-posed.

Modern hardware and compilers may reorder operations for performance, often relying on assumed associativity, and may even choose evaluation orders that vary across executions. This can violate the conditions above, even when the model is syntactically recurrent.

Discretization and evaluation order are not mere afterthoughts; they fundamentally determine the architecture’s expressivity. This can have surprising consequences. For instance, Merrill et al. (2024, Theorem 4.2) implies that RNNs without nonlinearity cannot simulate arbitrary finite machines. However, the theorem assumes a word-level evaluation order that does not satisfy condition 2, meaning it is not recurrence-consistent. It can be shown that, under different implementation semantics with consistent evaluation order, nominally linear recurrences are sufficient to simulate arbitrary finite machines. See Appendix H for details.

5 Conclusion

The paper establishes an algebraic characterization of recurrent language models in which the arithmetic semantics is part of the object characterized. For any model with recurrence-consistent evaluation, the global dynamics factor through the wreath product of the layer transition monoids; the syntactic monoid of any recognized language thereby divides this realized wreath product. Expressivity questions reduce to divisibility statements in a family of finite monoids, decidable via Krohn–Rhodes decomposition.

The stratification (cores, wirings, arithmetic) isolates the arithmetic semantics as the single component on which the realized monoids depend. The diagonal-SSM case study makes this concrete: the same idealized recurrence supports no modular counting under nonnegative floating-point arithmetic, yet recognizes parity under unsigned-integer quantization. The result of Sarrof et al. (2024) on the impossibility of parity in nonnegative diagonal SSMs is recovered as an instance of the divisibility chain.

The same algebraic analysis applies, with some adaptation, to attention-based architectures once attention is formalized as a recurrence, a direction we leave for future work.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank the anonymous reviewers for their valuable remarks and suggestions.

Impact Statement

This paper presents theoretical work aimed at advancing the field of machine learning by providing a procedure for understanding the formal capabilities of language models, which may also lead to the discovery of limitations and, in turn, to more capable architectures. Hence, as with any machine learning research, there are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Appendix B A Structural Perspective

The paper’s algebraic account sits between two hierarchies the literature has historically kept apart: the analytic hierarchy of real-valued recurrent architectures, and the algebraic hierarchy of finite-state automata. The bridge between them, discretization, is usually treated as a numerical perturbation absorbed by an ε\varepsilon. This is a category error in the technical sense: it confuses two structurally distinct levels.

A natural reflex is to organize the situation as a functor ℱ𝔐:ℝ​-​𝐑𝐍𝐍→𝐅𝐢𝐧​-​𝐑𝐍𝐍\mathcal{F}_{\mathfrak{M}}\colon\mathbb{R}\text{-}\mathbf{RNN}\to\mathbf{Fin}\text{-}\mathbf{RNN} from real-valued to finite-state RNNs, parameterized by an arithmetic 𝔐\mathfrak{M}. This picture is wrong structurally: ℱ\mathcal{F} does not preserve composition. For state updates f,gf,g over ℝ\mathbb{R},

ℱ⁡(g∘f)≠ℱ⁡(g)∘ℱ⁡(f),\mathcal{F}(g\circ f)\neq\mathcal{F}(g)\circ\mathcal{F}(f),

because rounding does not distribute over composition. The local loss of associativity in 𝔐\mathfrak{M} (Section 4) is the global non-functoriality of ℱ\mathcal{F}. A theorem in ℝ​-​𝐑𝐍𝐍\mathbb{R}\text{-}\mathbf{RNN} that relies on associativity, the chain of compositions underlying Siegelmann–Sontag Turing-completeness (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1992), for instance, does not transfer to 𝐅𝐢𝐧​-​𝐑𝐍𝐍\mathbf{Fin}\text{-}\mathbf{RNN} without a new proof carried out in the discrete setting. What survives, once 𝔐\mathfrak{M} is fixed, is the realized transition monoid Mℱ⁡(ℛ)e⁡(Σ)M_{\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{R})}^{e(\Sigma)} of Definition 3.10: a finite object carrying its own monoid structure inherited from 𝔐\mathfrak{M}, and the algebraic invariant that any syntactic monoid of a recognized language must divide.

Two consequences follow, each correcting a claim common in the literature. First, real-valued expressivity is not a lower bound on discrete expressivity: the Siegelmann–Sontag construction, discretized underfixed-evaluation floating-point, lands in a strictly subregular pseudovariety. Second, discrete expressivity is not a corruption of real-valued expressivity: wraparound integer arithmetic makes available cyclic group structure that real arithmetic does not naturally realize. Discretization does not project expressivity downward; it maps it onto a different pseudovariety, determined by 𝔐\mathfrak{M}.

Real-valued expressivity is an ideal; discrete expressivity is what computes. The translation between them cannot be analyzed at the level of morphisms in any meaningful category, because the proposed functor is not one. What can be analyzed are the algebraic invariants of ℱ⁡(ℛ)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{R}): its realized transition monoid and the pseudovariety it inhabits. These invariants were the object of the present paper, and of the case studies that follow.

Appendix C Limitations

This paper establishes expressivity rather than learnability: it asks whether there exists a specific parametrization of a given architecture from a family that can recognize a given formal language under a fixed numerical semantics. However, it makes no claims about whether such a parametrization could be found automatically through gradient-based optimization.

The present treatment is restricted to finite-precision semantics. As a result, every induced transition monoid is finite, and every recognized language is at most regular. The construction could be extended to account for settings in which precision or depth grows with input length, thereby yielding infinite monoids and enabling the architecture to capture non-regular languages.

Furthermore, the paper focuses on explicitly recurrent architectures, such as Elman-RNNs and structured state-space models. However, transformers are currently the dominant language model architecture, raising the question of whether the algebraic construction of this paper could be adapted to attention-based architectures as well. To fit the abstraction of transformation monoids established here, transformers would need to be formalized as recurrent models, which is natural for linear attention and certain finite-precision implementations, but requires further work.

Lastly, the paper focuses on establishing a purely algebraic abstraction of recurrent neural models and demonstrates its applicability through a case study of discrete diagonal state-space models. While this rederives and corrects known expressivity results about an important practical architecture, the paper does not attempt to prove fundamentally novel results about the expressivity of the plethora of other sequence-model architectures existing in the literature.

Appendix E Proof of the Factorization Lemma

We restate and prove the factorization lemma of Section 3.5. The proof is by induction on the depth NN of ℛ\mathcal{R} and rest on a single observation: the input xn+1x_{n+1} delivered to layer n+1n+1 depends on the states of the lower layers before they update on the current symbol, never after. This is precisely the dependency pattern encoded by the left-wreath-product convention of Section 2, where a wreath element (m,ϕ)(m,\phi) acts as (q,q′)↦(m⋅q,ϕ⁡(q)⋅q′)(q,q^{\prime})\mapsto(m\cdot q,\phi(q)\cdot q^{\prime}), with ϕ\phi evaluated at the old lower state.

See 3.12

(Fℛ)t​(q1)=f1​(q1,t)=(f1)t​(q1).(F_{\mathcal{R}})_{t}(q_{1})=f_{1}(q_{1},t)=(f_{1})_{t}(q_{1}).

MℛT=⟨(Fℛ)t∣t∈T⟩mon≤WℛT.M_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}=\bigl\langle(F_{\mathcal{R}})_{t}\mid t\in T\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\leq W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}.

Appendix F Proof of the Cascade Juxtaposition as Wreath Extension

See 3.20

Proof.

Throughout the proof, we write ℛ′′=defℛ⊳τℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\mathcal{R}\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}\mathcal{R}^{\prime} for brevity, and abbreviate ⋅\cdot for ⊳τ\mathbin{\rhd_{\tau}}, the wiring being fixed by hypothesis.

The wreath identity.

By Definition 3.5, ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime} is the algebraic RNN of depth N+N′N+N^{\prime} whose sequence of pairs is the concatenation of those of ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}, with τ\tau inserted as the wiring of the first core of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}. The realized wreath product Wℛ′′TW_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T} is then, by Definition 3.11, the iterated wreath product

𝕎ℛ′′T=(M1T,Q1)≀(M2T,Q2)≀⋯≀(MN+N′T,QN+N′).\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}=(M_{1}^{T},Q_{1})\wr(M_{2}^{T},Q_{2})\wr\cdots\wr(M_{N+N^{\prime}}^{T},Q_{N+N^{\prime}}).

By Remark 2.10, the wreath product of transformation monoids is associative up to canonical isomorphism. Grouping the first NN factors and the last N′N^{\prime} factors yields

𝕎ℛ′′T≅((M1T,Q1)≀⋯≀(MNT,QN))≀((MN+1T,QN+1)≀⋯≀(MN+N′T,QN+N′)).\mathbb{W}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}\cong\Bigl((M_{1}^{T},Q_{1})\wr\cdots\wr(M_{N}^{T},Q_{N})\Bigr)\wr\Bigl((M_{N+1}^{T},Q_{N+1})\wr\cdots\wr(M_{N+N^{\prime}}^{T},Q_{N+N^{\prime}})\Bigr).

The left bracket is WℛTW_{\mathcal{R}}^{T} by Definition 3.11 applied to ℛ\mathcal{R} and the set TT. The right bracket is the realized wreath product of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} relative to the inputs delivered by τ\tau through the cascade, that is, Wℛ′TW_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T} in the sense of the proposition’s statement. Hence the asserted identity, modulo the canonical isomorphism.

The inclusion in the wreath product.

The inclusion Mℛ′′T≤Wℛ′′T=WℛT≀Wℛ′TM_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}\leq W_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}=W_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\wr W_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}^{T} is Lemma 3.12 applied to ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime} with generating set TT.

The division.

For the division MℛT≺Mℛ′′TM_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}\prec M_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}, consider the projection π≤N:Qℛ′′→Qℛ\pi_{\leq N}\colon Q_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}\to Q_{\mathcal{R}} onto the first NN coordinates of the global state. The strictly feedforward wiring of the cascade (Definition 3.9) ensures that the dynamics on the first NN coordinates are independent of the remaining N′N^{\prime} coordinates: for every t∈Tt\in T and every (q≤N,q>N)∈Qℛ′′(q_{\leq N},q_{>N})\in Q_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}},

π≤N​((Fℛ′′)t​(q≤N,q>N))=(Fℛ)t​(q≤N).\pi_{\leq N}\!\bigl((F_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}})_{t}(q_{\leq N},q_{>N})\bigr)=(F_{\mathcal{R}})_{t}(q_{\leq N}).

The projection therefore induces a surjective monoid morphism π≤N∗:Mℛ′′T↠MℛT\pi_{\leq N}^{*}\colon M_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}\twoheadrightarrow M_{\mathcal{R}}^{T}, exhibiting MℛTM_{\mathcal{R}}^{T} as a quotient of Mℛ′′TM_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}}^{T}. This is the asserted division. ∎

Appendix G Models of Arithmetic

In the following, we outline the main arithmetic models used to analyze the expressivity of neural architectures. Critically, we point out the tradeoffs between space requirements and the cost of losing algebraic properties (most importantly, associativity).

G.1 Reals and Rationals

One common choice for expressivity analysis is to assume that all values lie in a field such as the real numbers ℝ\mathbb{R} or the rationals ℚ\mathbb{Q}. This may not be a realistic model for actual neural network implementations, because a given real number may not be representable in finite memory, and rationals may also have non-terminating binary expansions. Note that any specific rational number can be represented with finite space via an integer enumerator and denominator.

G.2 Floating-Point Arithmetic

By far the most common arithmetic model used to approximate real numbers by computer hardware is floating-point arithmetic. In this model, each of a finite subset of the real numbers is represented as the product of a sign ±\pm, a significand mm, and an integer power of a base bb (usually 22).22 2 Note that only numbers whose base-bb expansion terminates are exactly representable in that base with finitely many digits. For example, the fraction 1/31/3 cannot be exactly represented in base 22. The arithmetic model is specified by the precision pp (the number of digits in the significand) and an integer exponent range [emin,emax][e_{\min},e_{\max}].

The significand mm is a fractional value composed of pp digits (d0,d1,…,dp−1d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{p-1}) in base bb. Ignoring special values for the moment, floating-point numbers have the form:

±d0.d1​d2​…​dp−1⏟significand×b⏟basee⏞exponent\pm\underbrace{d_{0}.d_{1}d_{2}\dots d_{p-1}}_{\text{significand}}\times\underbrace{b}_{\text{base}}\overbrace{\vphantom{b}{}^{e}}^{\text{exponent}}

where emin≤e≤emaxe_{\min}\leq e\leq e_{\max} and 0≤di<b0\leq d_{i}<b for all i<pi<p. A floating-point number is called normal if d0≠0d_{0}\neq 0. In binary (b=2b=2), this implies d0=1d_{0}=1. Otherwise, it is called a subnormal number, if d0=0d_{0}=0 and the exponent is fixed at e=emine=e_{\min}. Subnormals extend the representable set of numbers toward 00 by trading significant bits of the mantissa for more space to represent smaller exponents.33 3 Note that in floating-point, 0 is not unique, since both +0+0 and −0-0 are valid distinct floating-point numbers.

Overflow and error behavior.

With any numerical system based on a finite set, an important question is what happens when operations result in values outside that range. In floating-point, numbers whose magnitude is larger than the maximum/minimum representable value result in overflow of dedicated infinity values (+∞+\infty and −∞-\infty). Adding or multiplying any normal or subnormal floating-point number with ±∞\pm\infty yields ±∞\pm\infty.

For results of invalid computations such as 0/00/0, ∞−∞\infty-\infty, etc. floating-point has NaNs (Not-a-Number). Note that this can also result from the denominator becoming 0 due to underflow. NaNs propagate, meaning that if at any point in a computation a subresult is NaN, the result of the whole computation will be NaN.

Rounding.

For any real number xx, let □⁡(x)\square(x) denote its floating-point rounding to the nearest representable value.44 4 Other rounding modes exist (toward 00, toward ±∞\pm\infty, stochastic rounding, etc.). The dominant default in scientific computing is round-to-nearest, with ties broken by the ties-to-even rule. Rounding introduces a small relative error with respect to the ambient system (ℝ\mathbb{R}) in which floating-point numbers are embedded when the result falls within the normal range. A standard abstraction for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} is:

□⁡(x)=x⁡(1+δ),|δ|≤u,\square(x)=x(1+\delta),\qquad|\delta|\leq u,

where uu is the unit roundoff (u=12​b1−pu=\frac{1}{2}b^{1-p} for round-to-nearest). The spacing between adjacent representable numbers grows with |x||x|, so floating point has roughly constant relative precision across magnitudes.

Floating-point arithmetic implements the basic operations {+,−,×,÷}\{+,-,\times,\div\} as if computing the real result and then rounding it back into the format with some rounding error δ\delta:

□(a⊙b)=(a⊙b)(1+δ),⊙∈{+,−,×,÷}\square(a\odot b)=(a\odot b)(1+\delta),\quad\odot\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}

In typical implementations, rounding occurs after each primitive operation; long multi-term computations therefore accumulate rounding error over many steps.

Rounding and overflow break associativity.

Rounding is fundamentally at odds with associativity, because the results of computations can differ depending on their order. This happens, for example, when a subterm adds two numbers, one of which is much smaller than the other, so the smaller one disappears. This is called absorption.

Example G.1 (Absorption).

Consider x=224−224+1=1x=2^{24}-2^{24}+1=1. In 32-bit floating-point, depending on ordering, this yields:

  1. (i)

    □⁡(□⁡(224−224)+1)=□⁡(0+1)=1\square(\square(2^{24}-2^{24})+1)=\square(0+1)=1

  2. (ii)

    □⁡(224−□⁡(224+1)=□⁡(224−224)=0CLOSE\square(2^{24}-\square(2^{24}+1)=\square(2^{24}-2^{24})=0

Another reason for associativity to fail in floating-point is overflow and error behavior.

Example G.2 (Overflow).

Let fmaxf_{\max} be the largest representable number smaller than ∞\infty in a given floating-point arithmetic. Then x=fmax+1−1x=f_{\max}+1-1 evaluates to:

  1. (i)

    □⁡(□⁡(fmax+1)−1)=□⁡(∞+1)=∞\square(\square(f_{\max}+1)-1)=\square(\infty+1)=\infty

  2. (ii)

    □⁡(fmax+□⁡(1−1)=□⁡(fmax+0)=fmaxCLOSE\square(f_{\max}+\square(1-1)=\square(f_{\max}+0)=f_{\max}

For similar reasons, rounding also breaks distributivity, meaning that in general:

□⁡((x⋅□⁡(y+z))≠□⁡(□⁡(x⋅y)+□⁡(x⋅z))CLOSE\square((x\cdot\square(y+z))\neq\square(\square(x\cdot y)+\square(x\cdot z))
Definition G.3 (Magma).

A magma is a set SS closed under a binary operation ⋅\cdot, not necessarily associative.

The algebraic structure formed by fixed-precision floating-point arithmetic is an ordered magma, an algebraic object with almost no structure.55 5 More specifically, it is an ordered commutative unital magma for ++ and ×\times and an ordered right-unital magma for −- and ÷\div when disregarding NaNs. Note that ordering is not strict due to absorption.

Definition G.4 (Ordered magma).

An ordered magma is a magma (S,⋅)(S,\cdot) together with a partial order ≤\leq on SS such that the binary operation is monotone in both arguments: for all a,b,c∈Sa,b,c\in S,

a≤b⟹a⋅c≤b⋅canda≤b⟹c⋅a≤c⋅b.a\leq b\implies a\cdot c\leq b\cdot c\quad\text{and}\quad a\leq b\implies c\cdot a\leq c\cdot b.

Equivalently, ⋅:S×S→S\cdot:S\times S\to S is order-preserving with respect to the product order on S×SS\times S.

In fact, in order for composite computations in a magma to be well-defined at all, we need to fix an execution order, such as always computing terms of the same precedence from left to right.

Remark G.5.

Most expressivity analyses in the literature treat fixed-precision arithmetic, such as floating-point arithmetic, as essentially ”Real arithmetic plus ϵ\epsilon”, where all analyses are done over ℝ\mathbb{R} and a small error is accounted for in the end. This does not work for formal language theory results, because rounding errors cannot be kept arbitrarily small in the general case (e.g., catastrophic cancellation, Goldberg (1991)). Furthermore, formal language theory handles arbitrarily long sequences, which means error accumulation can grow arbitrarily large for any non-zero marginal error.

Note also that the failure of distributivity makes matrix multiplication non-associative in floating-point arithmetic, meaning that regroupings of matrix- or tensor products for computational efficiency will generally not be arithmetically equivalent.

G.3 Integers

Another common model is integer arithmetic (quantization), which has been used successfully for efficient RNN inference (Jacob et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2021; Sari et al., 2021) and training (Wang et al., 2022; Nia et al., 2023). In contrast to floating-point arithmetic, integer-only arithmetic represents numbers as fixed-width bit words that map directly to the set of integers ℤ\mathbb{Z}. In this model, a value x∈ℤx\in\mathbb{Z} is represented by a bit word of length pp (the precision). Most modern hardware supports p∈{8,16,32,64}p\in\{8,16,32,64\}.

Overflow behavior.

For fixed-size integers, let denote the map that sends any integer to the bounded interval of representable values. For a fixed precision, integer arithmetic on standard hardware typically follows the rules of modular arithmetic, i.e., overflow is handled by wrap-around. In this case, for a precision pp, the result of an operation ⊙∈{+,−,×}\odot\in\{+,-,\times\} is:

  ​(x⊙y)=x⊙y(mod2p)\hbox to6.86pt{\vbox to6.86pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 3.43144pt\lower-3.43144pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 4.47 0 C 4.47 2.47 2.47 4.47 0 4.47 C -2.47 4.47 -4.47 2.47 -4.47 0 C -4.47 -2.47 -2.47 -4.47 0 -4.47 C 2.47 -4.47 4.47 -2.47 4.47 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-2.42361pt}{-2.15277pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.35 -2.98)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}} \lxSVG@closescope }}} } \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}(x\odot y)=x\odot y\pmod{2^{p}}

A common alternative to handle overflow in integer arithmetic, especially in machine learning, is to clamp to the lowest value imini_{\min} or the highest value imaxi_{\max} at the boundaries of the interval.

  ​(x⊙y)=min⁡(max⁡(x⊙y,imin),imax)\hbox to6.86pt{\vbox to6.86pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 3.43144pt\lower-3.43144pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 4.47 0 C 4.47 2.47 2.47 4.47 0 4.47 C -2.47 4.47 -4.47 2.47 -4.47 0 C -4.47 -2.47 -2.47 -4.47 0 -4.47 C 2.47 -4.47 4.47 -2.47 4.47 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-2.42361pt}{-2.15277pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.35 -2.98)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}} \lxSVG@closescope }}} } \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}(x\odot y)=\min(\max(x\odot y,i_{\min}),i_{\max})
Associativity.

The algebraic consequences of overflow handling in integer arithmetic depend sharply on whether wrap-around or clamping is used, and on whether the integers are signed or unsigned.

Wrap-around induces exact modular arithmetic over ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}, where pp is the precision. In this case, addition and multiplication are associative and distributive, yielding a commutative ring (for addition and multiplication) and hence a well-structured algebra.

Clamped arithmetic behaves fundamentally differently. For signed integers, clamping breaks associativity:

in general, because intermediate results may saturate at imini_{\min} or imaxi_{\max} depending on evaluation order. Distributivity over multiplication also fails for the same reason. The resulting structure is only a commutative ordered unital bimagma: closure and commutativity hold, but associativity and distributivity do not.

For unsigned integers, clamping preserves associativity of addition and multiplication, since saturation occurs only at a single boundary and cannot be crossed in the opposite direction. In this case, clamped arithmetic forms a commutative ordered bimonoid: associativity and units are preserved, but inverses are absent. In this case, the resulting algebra is a strictly ordered commutative magma.

Crucially, even when scalar associativity is preserved (as in unsigned clamped arithmetic), matrix associativity fails in all clamped settings. Matrix multiplication relies on distributivity to rearrange sums of products; clamping inside the scalar operations breaks this property, so in general

(A​B)​C≠A⁡(B​C)(AB)C\neq A(BC)

As a result, clamped integer arithmetic does not admit a well-defined matrix monoid without fixing an execution order, mirroring the situation for floating-point arithmetic.

Unbounded Integers

Modern programming languages like Python include integer datatypes that can grow arbitrarily large. This means there is no possibility for overflow and hence no need to define wrap-around or saturation behavior. The resulting algebraic structure is simply the ring of integers ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Note that unbounded integer representations of recurrent hidden states can grow linearly in the sequence length.

G.4 Fixed-Point Precision

Another common model is fixed-point arithmetic. We will not focus on it here, as it does not introduce unique algebraic structures and is effectively an intermediate between floating-point and integer arithmetic. In this model, each number is represented as a scaled integer, with the radix point (decimal or binary) fixed in a consistent position across all values and operations. Results are rounded or truncated to ensure they remain within the representable set. Consequently, fixed-point inherits the rounding complexities and non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic; however, these issues are often more pronounced because the rounding error is absolute (constant) rather than relative to the magnitude of the value. Ultimately, it can be viewed as an extension of integer arithmetic, in which the unit of least precision is shifted by a fixed scaling factor.

Appendix H Example: Clamped Linear Recurrence

The written recurrence of an RNN layer alone does not determine the implemented transition map. In particular, a source-level affine update may become nonlinear once finite-precision semantics are fixed. This is not merely a pathological possibility: in standard fixed-point and integer-only implementations, matrix products are typically accumulated in a wider register and then requantized or saturated when cast back to the target format, so clamping already appears as part of realistic execution semantics (Jacob et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2021). The crucial issue is therefore not whether clamping occurs, but where the clamp barriers occur in the staged implementation.

To make this explicit, compare the usual Elman recurrence (Eq. D.2, where we choose ReLU\mathrm{ReLU} for σq\sigma_{q})

f⁡(qt−1,xt)=ReLU⁡(Wq​qt−1+Uq​xt+bq),f(q_{t-1},x_{t})=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{q}q_{t-1}+U_{q}x_{t}+b_{q}), (H.20)

with the source-level affine update

f⁡(qt−1,xt)=A​qt−1+B​xt+b1+b2+b3,f(q_{t-1},x_{t})=Aq_{t-1}+Bx_{t}+b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}, (H.21)

where qt−1,qt,bi∈ℝdq_{t-1},q_{t},b_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for 0≤i≤3,d∈ℝ+0\leq i\leq 3,d\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, xt∈ℝnx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, Wq,A∈ℝd×d,Uq,B∈ℤd×nW_{q},A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},U_{q},B\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times n}, and t,n,d,q∈ℤ+t,n,d,q\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}.

Syntactically, the latter update contains no nonlinearity. Now fix a consistent evaluation order and a staged clamped signed-integer semantics with coordinatewise saturation
