Intuitively, the gadget “subtract cc, clamp, add cc” turns the lower saturation boundary into a zeroing threshold: negative values are pushed to −c-c and return as 00, while positive values remain in the unsaturated regime and survive unchanged.

Corollary H.2.

Any DFA simulation theorem for ReLU Elman recurrences using bounded-range integers transfers to this staged clamped affine model.

Proof.

Classical threshold-network constructions, dating back to Minsky, show how finite dynamics can be embedded in recurrent networks via thresholding. For the bounded finite-precision setting relevant here, Korsky and Berwick (2019) show constructively that finite-precision single-layer ReLU recurrences are exactly as computationally powerful as deterministic finite automata, using only integers in a bounded range. By Proposition H.1, each such ReLU update can be replaced, within the same bounded working region, by the staged clamped affine update above. Therefore, the same hidden-state transition system, and hence the same DFA simulation, is realized. ∎

Note that this only apparently contradicts prior limitations for linear recurrences (e.g., Merrill et al., 2024, Theorem 4.2). Those results assume computational semantics under which the recurrence remains genuinely linear and also follow a recurrence-consistent evaluation strategy. By contrast, we show that whether a recurrence is genuinely linear cannot be read off from the written formula alone. Once finite-precision clamping is part of the operational semantics, a nominally affine recurrence may already contain the thresholding nonlinearity on which classical automata simulations rely.

Appendix I Krohn–Rhodes Theorem

Here, we briefly state a transformation-monoid version of the Krohn–Rhodes theorem (Krohn and Rhodes, 1965).

We first recall the two kinds of prime transformation monoids that occur in the decomposition.

Definition I.1.

The flip-flop is the transformation monoid

FF=def(U3,{qa,qb}),\textsc{FF}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}(U_{3},\{q_{a},q_{b}\}),

where U3=def{Id,a,b}U_{3}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\{\mathrm{Id},a,b\} consists of the identity transformation together with the two constant transformations

a⁡(q)=qa,b⁡(q)=qb,∀q∈{qa,qb}.a(q)=q_{a},\qquad b(q)=q_{b},\qquad\forall q\in\{q_{a},q_{b}\}.

Its transition monoid has the following multiplication table:

U3IdabIdIdabaaabbbab\begin{array}[]{c|ccc}U_{3}&\mathrm{Id}&a&b\\ \hline\cr\mathrm{Id}&\mathrm{Id}&a&b\\ a&a&a&b\\ b&b&a&b\end{array}

where composition is read in the convention used throughout this paper.

Definition I.2.

A prime transformation group is a transformation monoid (G,G)(G,G) where GG is a nontrivial finite simple group acting faithfully on itself by right multiplication.

Thus, the prime transformation groups are exactly

{(G,G)∣G​ is a nontrivial finite simple group}.\{(G,G)\mid G\text{ is a nontrivial finite simple group}\}.

Equivalently, the possible groups GG are the non-abelian finite simple groups together with the cyclic groups ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{p}\mathbb{Z} of prime order pp.

Theorem I.3 (Krohn–Rhodes).

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a finite transformation monoid. Then there exist transformation monoids

(M1,Q1),…,(Mk,Qk)(M_{1},Q_{1}),\ldots,(M_{k},Q_{k})

such that each (Mi,Qi)(M_{i},Q_{i}) is either the flip-flop FF or a prime transformation group (Gi,Gi)(G_{i},G_{i}), and

(M,X)≺(M1,Q1)≀(M2,Q2)≀⋯≀(Mk,Qk).(M,X)\prec(M_{1},Q_{1})\wr(M_{2},Q_{2})\wr\cdots\wr(M_{k},Q_{k}).

That is, every finite transformation monoid divides an iterated wreath product of flip-flops and prime transformation groups.

Appendix J Case Study: Diagonal State Space Models

This section instantiates the algebraic theory of Section 3 on diagonal SSMs with input-dependent transitions, in the spirit of Sarrof et al. (2024). The same idealized recurrence is analyzed under several arithmetic models, and the resulting expressivity differs from one model to the next.

J.1 Architecture specification

The diagonal SSM is an algebraic RNN in the sense of Definition 3.4. To make the translation between the two transparent, the symbols of the algebraic core (Definition 3.1) are reused verbatim: the state, input, and readout sets are Qn,Xn,YnQ_{n},X_{n},Y_{n}, the transition and readout maps are fn,gnf_{n},g_{n}, and the wiring is τn\tau_{n}. Every algebraic statement of Section 3 thus translates to the present setting by direct substitution.

Fix integers N,m,d∈ℤ+N,m,d\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, where NN is the depth, mm the hidden dimension, and dd the model dimension. For each layer n∈{1,…,N}n\in\{1,\dots,N\}, set Qn=ℝmQ_{n}=\mathbb{R}^{m} and Xn=Yn=ℝdX_{n}=Y_{n}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. Write Diagm⊆ℝm×m\mathrm{Diag}_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} for the ring of diagonal m×mm\times m real matrices, and identify a diagonal matrix with its diagonal vector, Diagm≅ℝm\mathrm{Diag}_{m}\cong\mathbb{R}^{m}. Write Diagm+≅Diagm\mathrm{Diag}_{m}^{+}\cong\mathrm{Diag}_{m} for the sub-semiring of diagonals with nonnegative values.

The layer is parameterized by three learned maps, not assumed linear,

An:ℝd→Diagm,Bn:ℝd→ℝm×d,Cn:ℝd→ℝd×m,A_{n}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathrm{Diag}_{m},\qquad B_{n}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times d},\qquad C_{n}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},

assigning to each input the diagonal transition matrix, the input matrix, and the readout matrix. The recurrence and readout maps fn:Qn×Xn→Qnf_{n}\colon Q_{n}\times X_{n}\to Q_{n} and gn:Qn×Xn→Yng_{n}\colon Q_{n}\times X_{n}\to Y_{n} are, for every t≥1t\geq 1, every qt−1∈ℝmq_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and every xt∈ℝdx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

fn​(qt−1,xt)\displaystyle f_{n}(q_{t-1},x_{t}) =An​(xt)​qt−1+Bn​(xt)​xt,\displaystyle=A_{n}(x_{t})\,q_{t-1}+B_{n}(x_{t})\,x_{t}, (J.23)
gn​(qt,xt)\displaystyle g_{n}(q_{t},x_{t}) =Cn​(xt)​qt.\displaystyle=C_{n}(x_{t})\,q_{t}. (J.24)

The wiring map τn:Xn×Yn→Xn+1\tau_{n}\colon X_{n}\times Y_{n}\to X_{n+1} is, for x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

τn​(x,y)=norm⁡(ReLU⁡(x​M)​y)+x,\tau_{n}(x,y)=\mathrm{norm}\!\bigl(\mathrm{ReLU}(x\,M)\,y\bigr)+x,

where M∈ℝd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a parameter, ϵ∈ℝ>0\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} is a fixed stabilization constant, and, for 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d,

ReLU​(x)i=max⁡(0,xi),norm​(x)i=xi1d​∑j=1dxj2+ϵ.\mathrm{ReLU}(x)_{i}=\max(0,x_{i}),\qquad\mathrm{norm}(x)_{i}=\frac{x_{i}}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{j}^{2}+\epsilon}}.

The encoder and decoder are set maps e:Σ→ℝde\colon\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}^{d} and d:ℝd→{0,1}d\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\{0,1\}, where Σ\Sigma is the finite input alphabet. The encoder factors through the one-hot embedding Σ↪ℝ|Σ|\Sigma\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{|\Sigma|} followed by a linear map ℝ|Σ|→ℝd\mathbb{R}^{|\Sigma|}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}; this is a factorization, not a linearity assumption on ee, since Σ\Sigma carries no vector-space structure.

Definition J.1 (Nonnegative diagonal SSM).

A diagonal SSM is nonnegative if every transition matrix it produces has nonnegative entries, that is, An:ℝd→Diagm+A_{n}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathrm{Diag}_{m}^{+}, for every nn.66 6 This is close to Mamba, with ReLU\mathrm{ReLU} in place of SiLU and no convolution across time.

J.2 Discretization

The expressivity question is well-posed only after the numerical semantics that turns each symbolic recurrence into a total function has been fixed. Fix an arithmetic model 𝔐\mathfrak{M} (Definition 4.2) with finite representable set Q𝔐⊆ℝQ_{\mathfrak{M}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, so that the layer state set is Qn𝔐=Q𝔐mQ_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}=Q_{\mathfrak{M}}^{m} and the encoder takes values in Q𝔐dQ_{\mathfrak{M}}^{d}. For diagonal SSM updates, the evaluation tree of Eq. J.23 is fixed coordinatewise (Definition 4.3): at coordinate ii, the multiplication An​(x)i,i​qiA_{n}(x)_{i,i}\,q_{i} is evaluated before the addition with the precomputed constant bi𝔐​(x)=def⟦Bn​(x)​x⟧𝔐|i∈Q𝔐b_{i}^{\mathfrak{M}}(x)\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\llbracket B_{n}(x)\,x\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\big|_{i}\in Q_{\mathfrak{M}}, and Definition 4.2 prescribes a rounding at each of these two nodes:

⟦fn​(q,x)⟧𝔐|i=□⁡(□⁡(An​(x)i,i​qi)+bi𝔐​(x)).\llbracket f_{n}(q,x)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}}\big|_{i}=\square\!\bigl(\square(A_{n}(x)_{i,i}\,q_{i})+b_{i}^{\mathfrak{M}}(x)\bigr).

The induced map

(Fn)x𝔐:Qn𝔐→Qn𝔐,(Fn)x𝔐​(q)=def⟦fn​(q,x)⟧𝔐,(F_{n})_{x}^{\mathfrak{M}}\colon Q_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}\to Q_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}},\qquad(F_{n})_{x}^{\mathfrak{M}}(q)\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\llbracket f_{n}(q,x)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{M}},

is total for every admissible input x∈Xn𝔐=defe⁡(Σ)⊆Q𝔐dx\in X_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}e(\Sigma)\subseteq Q_{\mathfrak{M}}^{d}, on the standing assumption that every realizable parameter choice yields a self-map of Q𝔐Q_{\mathfrak{M}}, producing in particular no NaN. The core transition monoid is

Mn𝔐=def⟨(Fn)x𝔐:x∈Xn𝔐⟩mon≤(Qn𝔐)Qn𝔐,M_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl\langle(F_{n})_{x}^{\mathfrak{M}}:x\in X_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\leq(Q_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}})^{Q_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}},

Arithmetic models.

Two models are used below. fp denotes a fixed finite floating-point format of IEEE type, with its induced finite set of representable values. intp\textsc{int}^{p} denotes unsigned integer arithmetic with wraparound at pp bits, that is, the ring ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}.

Reduction to one coordinate.

Since An​(x)A_{n}(x) is diagonal, the update acts coordinatewise: for every x∈Xn𝔐x\in X_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}} and 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, the ii-th coordinate evolves under the one-dimensional affine self-map

Fa,b𝔐:Q𝔐→Q𝔐,q↦□⁡(□⁡(a​q)+b),F_{a,b}^{\mathfrak{M}}\colon Q_{\mathfrak{M}}\to Q_{\mathfrak{M}},\qquad q\mapsto\square\!\bigl(\square(aq)+b\bigr),

with a=defAn​(x)i,i∈Q𝔐a\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}A_{n}(x)_{i,i}\in Q_{\mathfrak{M}} and b=defbi𝔐​(x)∈Q𝔐b\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}b_{i}^{\mathfrak{M}}(x)\in Q_{\mathfrak{M}}. Let Πi=def{(An​(x)i,i,bi𝔐​(x)):x∈Xn𝔐}⊆Q𝔐×Q𝔐\Pi_{i}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\{(A_{n}(x)_{i,i},\,b_{i}^{\mathfrak{M}}(x)):x\in X_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}\}\subseteq Q_{\mathfrak{M}}\times Q_{\mathfrak{M}} collect the parameter pairs realizable at coordinate ii, and let Mi=def⟨Fa,b𝔐:(a,b)∈Πi⟩mon≤Q𝔐Q𝔐M_{i}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}\bigl\langle F_{a,b}^{\mathfrak{M}}:(a,b)\in\Pi_{i}\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\leq Q_{\mathfrak{M}}^{Q_{\mathfrak{M}}} be the monoid they generate. The coordinatewise action embeds the core monoid in the product, Mn𝔐≤M1×⋯×MmM_{n}^{\mathfrak{M}}\leq M_{1}\times\cdots\times M_{m}.

The one-dimensional analysis serves two distinct purposes. To exhibit a group inside a core, it suffices to display a single pair (a,b)∈Πi(a,b)\in\Pi_{i}, frozen on the other coordinates; this is an existence statement and uses a single generator (Lemmas J.5 and J.9). To bound the group content of a core, one must control the whole monoid MiM_{i}, hence all words in its generators; the bound holds word by word because the governing invariant, monotonicity or the parity of the number of negative multipliers, is stable under composition (Lemmas J.3 and J.6).

J.2.1 Floating point

Definition J.2.

A finite monoid MM is aperiodic if there exists N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} with mN=mN+1m^{N}=m^{N+1} for all m∈Mm\in M. The class of finite aperiodic monoids is the pseudovariety 𝐀𝐩\mathbf{Ap}.77 7 For a definition of pseudovarieties, see Eilenberg and Schützenberger (1976).

Lemma J.3 (Nonnegative floating-point updates are aperiodic).

Fix 𝔐=fp\mathfrak{M}=\textsc{fp} with NaNs excluded and a recurrence-consistent evaluation order. If every realizable one-dimensional update at a coordinate has a nonnegative multiplier, then the monoid MiM_{i} it generates is aperiodic.

Proof.

Let (Qfp,≤)(Q_{\textsc{fp}},\leq) be the finite set of IEEE 754 values, including ±∞\pm\infty and excluding NaNs, with its usual total order. Each generator has the form Fa,bfp​(q)=□⁡(□⁡(a​q)+b)F_{a,b}^{\textsc{fp}}(q)=\square(\square(aq)+b) with a≥0a\geq 0. IEEE 754 rounding preserves monotonicity for addition and multiplication under the fixed semantics (Mikaitis, 2024, Thms. II.1, II.3), so multiplication by a≥0a\geq 0, addition of bb, and both roundings are order-preserving, whence each generator is an order-preserving self-map of the finite chain. A composition of order-preserving maps is order-preserving, so every m∈Mim\in M_{i} is order-preserving. An order-preserving self-map of a finite chain has no nontrivial cycle: for any qq, the sequence (mk⋅q)k≥1(m^{k}\cdot q)_{k\geq 1} is monotone in a finite set, hence stabilizes after at most N=|Qfp|N=|Q_{\textsc{fp}}| steps, giving mN=mN+1m^{N}=m^{N+1}. Therefore Mi∈𝐀𝐩M_{i}\in\mathbf{Ap}. ∎

Corollary J.4 (Nonnegative floating-point cores are aperiodic).

Every nonnegative diagonal SSM core over fp, with NaNs excluded and fixed evaluation semantics, has an aperiodic transition monoid.

Proof.

By Lemma J.3, each coordinate monoid MiM_{i} is aperiodic, since the realizable multipliers An​(x)i,iA_{n}(x)_{i,i} are nonnegative. The core monoid embeds in M1×⋯×MmM_{1}\times\cdots\times M_{m} by the coordinatewise action. Finite products of aperiodic monoids are aperiodic, and submonoids inherit aperiodicity. ∎

Lemma J.5 (Signed floating-point cores contain ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}).

A diagonal SSM core over fp whose realizable multipliers include −1-1 contains a transition group isomorphic to ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

The set QfpQ_{\textsc{fp}} contains the negation-invariant subset {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}, on which negation is exact (treating +0+0 and −0-0 as equal under ≤\leq). The one-dimensional update with parameters a=−1a=-1, b=0b=0 then satisfies F−1,0fp∘F−1,0fp=IdF_{-1,0}^{\textsc{fp}}\circ F_{-1,0}^{\textsc{fp}}=\mathrm{Id} on {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}, so F−1,0fpF_{-1,0}^{\textsc{fp}} has order 22 there, while F1,0fp=IdF_{1,0}^{\textsc{fp}}=\mathrm{Id}. Hence ⟨F−1,0fp,F1,0fp⟩mon≅ℤ/2​ℤ\bigl\langle F_{-1,0}^{\textsc{fp}},F_{1,0}^{\textsc{fp}}\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}}\cong\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, embedded in the core monoid by freezing the remaining coordinates. ∎

Lemma J.6 (Group content of floating-point cores).

Let MiM_{i} be the monoid generated by one-dimensional affine floating-point updates at a coordinate, with NaNs excluded. Every subgroup of MiM_{i} is either trivial or isomorphic to ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

The governing invariant is order. For a>0a>0 the map Fa,bfp​(q)=□⁡(□⁡(a​q)+b)F_{a,b}^{\textsc{fp}}(q)=\square(\square(aq)+b) is order-preserving, and for a<0a<0 it is order-reversing, under the fixed semantics. Hence, a word in the generators is order-preserving or order-reversing according to the parity of the number of negative multipliers it contains, and every element of MiM_{i} is of one of these two kinds. Let G≤MiG\leq M_{i} be a subgroup with identity idempotent ee; then GG acts faithfully by permutations of the finite chain Im(e)=e⁡(Q)⊆Qfp\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(e)=e(Q)\subseteq Q_{\textsc{fp}}. The only order-preserving permutation of a finite chain is the identity, and there is at most one order-reversing one, the reversal, so |G|≤2|G|\leq 2. Thus, the only nontrivial group appearing is ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, whose instantiation was shown in Lemma J.5. ∎

Corollary J.7 (Floating-point cores have elementary abelian 22-group content).

Every diagonal SSM core over fp, with NaNs excluded, self-map updates, and arbitrary signed multipliers, has a transition monoid whose subgroups are elementary abelian 22-groups.

Proof.

By Lemma J.6, each coordinate monoid has only trivial or ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z} subgroups. The core monoid embeds in M1×⋯×MmM_{1}\times\cdots\times M_{m}, so each of its subgroups embeds in a product of copies of 11 and ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, hence is elementary abelian of exponent at most 22. ∎

J.2.2 Unsigned integers

Lemma J.8 (Unsigned integers contain aperiodic monoids).

For 𝔐=intp\mathfrak{M}=\textsc{int}^{p} the one-dimensional affine updates generate nontrivial aperiodic monoids.

Proof.

The update with a=2a=2, b=0b=0 is F⁡(q)=2​qmod2pF(q)=2q\bmod 2^{p}, which sends every state to 00 after pp iterations, so Fp=Fp+1F^{p}=F^{p+1} and ⟨F⟩mon\bigl\langle F\bigr\rangle_{\mathrm{mon}} is aperiodic. ∎

Lemma J.9 (Unsigned integers contain cyclic 22-groups).

For 𝔐=intp\mathfrak{M}=\textsc{int}^{p} and every k≤pk\leq p, the one-dimensional affine updates contain a cyclic group isomorphic to ℤ/2k​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2^{k}}\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

The translation F1,1intp​(q)=q+1mod2pF_{1,1}^{\textsc{int}^{p}}(q)=q+1\bmod 2^{p} is a single 2p2^{p}-cycle on ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}, hence a permutation of order 2p2^{p}. For k≤pk\leq p the step of size 2p−k2^{p-k} has order 2k2^{k}, giving an explicit copy of ℤ/2k​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2^{k}}\mathbb{Z}. ∎

Corollary J.10 (Unsigned-integer cores have 22-group content).

Every diagonal SSM core over intp\textsc{int}^{p} has a transition monoid whose subgroups are finite 22-groups, and a single core already realizes ℤ/2k​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2^{k}}\mathbb{Z} for every k≤pk\leq p.

Proof.

The bijective affine self-maps of ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z} are the maps q↦a​q+bq\mapsto aq+b with aa a unit of ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}, that is, with aa odd; they form the group AGL⁡(1,ℤ/2p​ℤ)\mathrm{AGL}(1,\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}),88 8 The affine general group of degree 11 over the ring ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}. of order 2p−1⋅2p=22​p−12^{p-1}\cdot 2^{p}=2^{2p-1}, a 22-group. An affine self-map q↦a​q+bq\mapsto aq+b is idempotent precisely when a2=aa^{2}=a and a​b=0ab=0 in ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}. In ℤ/2p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}, a2=aa^{2}=a forces a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}: either a=0a=0 (a constant map, with bb arbitrary), or a=1a=1 together with b=0b=0 (the identity). Let GG be a subgroup of a coordinate monoid, with identity idempotent ee. If ee is a constant map, GG acts faithfully on the singleton Im(e)\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(e) and is trivial; if e=Ide=\mathrm{Id}, then G≤AGL⁡(1,ℤ/2p​ℤ)G\leq\mathrm{AGL}(1,\mathbb{Z}/2^{p}\mathbb{Z}) and is a 22-group. Every subgroup of a coordinate monoid is therefore a 22-group, and the same holds for the core monoid, which embeds in the product of coordinate monoids. Realizability of ℤ/2k​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2^{k}}\mathbb{Z} is Lemma J.9. ∎

Reading the table.

The two regimes, signed fp and nonnegative intp\textsc{int}^{p}, realize the same pseudovariety at the level of a single core, 𝐀𝐩∨⟨ℤ/2​ℤ⟩\mathbf{Ap}\vee\langle\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}\rangle, even though their subgroup data differ. Krohn–Rhodes sees only the simple group divisors, and the only simple 22-group is ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}. The richer subgroup structure of an intp\textsc{int}^{p} core, namely cyclic 22-groups of any order up to 2p2^{p}, is therefore absorbed by the wreath-product closure. The difference between the two regimes is a depth-for-width trade within the same pseudovariety, made explicit in Remark J.15. Here, ∨\vee denotes the join of pseudovarieties, i.e., 𝐀∨𝐁\mathbf{A}\vee\mathbf{B} is the smallest pseudovariety containing pseudovarieties 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B}.

J.3 Upper bounds

The divisibility chain Eq. 3.1 turns each core-level fact above into a constraint on the recognized language. The accepting core of an SSM acceptor is memoryless: its state space is a singleton; hence, its transition monoid is trivial. By Corollary 3.21, the augmented wreath product therefore has the same group content as the base, and we omit the accepting core from the group-theoretic bookkeeping below.

Theorem J.11 (Nonnegative floating point).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an SSM acceptor whose base is a nonnegative diagonal SSM over fp with fixed evaluation semantics. Then M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) is aperiodic.

Proof.

By Corollary J.4, every core monoid lies in 𝐀𝐩\mathbf{Ap}. Since 𝐀𝐩\mathbf{Ap} is closed under wreath product, Wℛ+∈𝐀𝐩W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}\in\mathbf{Ap}. By Eq. 3.1, M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))≺Wℛ+M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}))\prec W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}, and 𝐀𝐩\mathbf{Ap} is closed under division. ∎

Example J.12.

The parity language ℒ={w∈{0,1}∗:w​ has an even number of ​1​s}\mathcal{L}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^{*}:w\text{ has an even number of }1\text{s}\} has syntactic monoid ℤ/2​ℤ∉𝐀𝐩\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}\notin\mathbf{Ap}. By Theorem J.11, no nonnegative diagonal SSM over fp recognizes ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Allowing the multiplier −1-1, as suggested by Sarrof et al. (2024), adds the factor ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z} but nothing beyond it.

Theorem J.13 (Signed floating point).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an SSM acceptor whose base is a diagonal SSM over fp with fixed evaluation semantics and arbitrary signed multipliers. Then every group divisor of M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) is isomorphic to ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}; equivalently, M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) divides a wreath product of flip-flops and copies of ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

By Corollary J.7, every core monoid has only elementary abelian 22-group subgroups, and the same therefore holds for Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} by closure under wreath product and division. A simple subgroup of an elementary abelian 22-group is trivial or ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, so the only nontrivial Krohn–Rhodes group factors (Theorem I.3) of Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} are copies of ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, and Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} divides a wreath product of flip-flops and copies of ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}. The conclusion follows from M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))≺Wℛ+M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}))\prec W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} (Eq. 3.1) and transitivity of division. ∎

Theorem J.14 (Unsigned integers).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an SSM acceptor whose base is a diagonal SSM over intp\textsc{int}^{p}. Then every group divisor of M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) is a finite 22-group; equivalently, M⁡(ℒ⁡(𝒜))M(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})) divides a wreath product of flip-flops and copies of ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

By Corollary J.10, every core monoid has only finite 22-group subgroups, and the same therefore holds for Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}}. A finite 22-group has ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z} as its only simple subquotient (since every pp-group has a nontrivial center), so the only nontrivial Krohn–Rhodes group factors of Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} are copies of ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, and Wℛ+W_{{\mathcal{R}^{+}}} divides a wreath product of flip-flops and copies of ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}. The conclusion follows from Eq. 3.1 and transitivity of division. ∎

Remark J.15 (Same languages, different depth).

Theorems J.13 and J.14 characterize the same class of languages: those whose syntactic monoid has only 22-groups as group divisors. The two regimes differ at the level of a single core, not of the language. A signed fp core realizes only elementary abelian 22-groups (Corollary J.7), so it produces ℤ/4​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{4}\mathbb{Z} only across two layers, through ℤ/4​ℤ≺ℤ/2​ℤ≀ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{4}\mathbb{Z}\prec\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}\wr\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}; an intp\textsc{int}^{p} core realizes ℤ/2k​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2^{k}}\mathbb{Z} within a single layer (Lemma J.9). The difference is thus a depth-for-width trade, and the algebraic view exhibits it as one.

Example J.16.

The language ℒ={w∈{0,1}∗:the number of ​1​s is a multiple of ​3}\mathcal{L}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\text{the number of }1\text{s is a multiple of }3\} has syntactic monoid ℤ/3​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{3}\mathbb{Z}. A group divisor of a monoid covered by Theorem J.13 or Theorem J.14 is a 22-group, and ℤ/3​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{3}\mathbb{Z} is not, so no diagonal SSM over fp or over intp\textsc{int}^{p} recognizes ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Corollary J.17.

For any integer kk that is not a power of 22, no diagonal SSM over fp or over intp\textsc{int}^{p} recognizes the language of words whose number of 11s is divisible by kk.

The same impossibility for fp follows, by a different route, from the eigenvalue analysis of Grazzi et al. (2025, Theorem 2).

J.4 A lower bound

The upper bounds leave room for parity under unsigned integers, and an explicit construction realizes it with a nonnegative recurrence.

Example J.18 (Parity over unsigned integers).

The parity language ℒ={w∈{0,1}∗:w​ has an even number of ​1​s}\mathcal{L}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^{*}:w\text{ has an even number of }1\text{s}\} is recognized by a nonnegative diagonal SSM over intp\textsc{int}^{p}.

Proof.

The syntactic monoid of ℒ\mathcal{L} is ℤ/2​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/{2}\mathbb{Z}, realizable by a single core by Lemma J.9, so it remains to give an explicit acceptor. Take one layer, N=1N=1, with m=d=1m=d=1 and 44-bit unsigned integers, so Q=X=Y=ℤ/16​ℤQ=X=Y=\mathbb{Z}/16\mathbb{Z}. Encode e⁡(0)=0e(0)=0 and e⁡(1)=1e(1)=1, and set A⁡(0)=A⁡(1)=1A(0)=A(1)=1, B⁡(0)=0B(0)=0, B⁡(1)=8B(1)=8, so the recurrence is

q′=A⁡(x)​q+B⁡(x)​x={q+8(mod16),x=1,q,x=0.q^{\prime}=A(x)\,q+B(x)\,x=\begin{cases}q+8\pmod{16},&x=1,\\ q,&x=0.\end{cases}

The transition matrix is nonnegative. Take initial state q0=15q_{0}=15, so a prefix with an even number of 11s yields state 1515, and one with an odd number yields state 77. Set C⁡(0)=C⁡(1)=1C(0)=C(1)=1, so the readout equals the state, and let the accepting core read the state alone, with accepting region {15}\{15\}. The empty word, having zero 11s, leaves the state at 1515 and is accepted, in agreement with ε∈ℒ\varepsilon\in\mathcal{L}, and a word w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*} is accepted exactly when its number of 11s is even. ∎

Read against Sarrof et al. (2024, Theorem 2), which states that no nonnegative diagonal SSM in finite precision recognizes parity, Example J.18 shows the claim to depend on the unstated assumption that the arithmetic is floating point: it holds over fp by Theorem J.11 and fails over intp\textsc{int}^{p}.

Finite against unbounded precision.

An SSM, all of whose layers have a finite state space, recognizes only regular languages, since a finite wreath product of finite monoids is finite and every language recognized by a finite monoid is regular. Unbounded precision changes the regime: an unbounded integer data type allows the core state to grow with the input, inducing an infinite, length-indexed monoid action and placing the model beyond the finite-automaton boundary, where non-regular behavior becomes available.
